articles.content: Climate activists at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey , awarded Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney a Fossil of the Day award , along with other leaders from wealthy countries who skipped the summit. The satirical award is given to countries and leaders seen as doing little to support efforts to tackle climate change. The award was not the only criticism of Carney’s climate credentials. Newsweek listed the prime minister at No. 2 on a list of “climate heretics,” just behind Microsoft founder Bill Gates and ahead of United States President Donald Trump. These criticisms might seem surprising, as Carney has been seen as a climate champion. At the 2015 COP in Paris , Carney said companies need to develop plans for net-zero emissions . Yet, after becoming prime minister, he scrapped the federal consumer carbon tax and signed an agreement with Alberta to push forward a new oil pipeline. How should we make sense of the Fossil of the Day award? How did Carney go from seeming climate hero to climate villain? As sociologists, we have written about and researched environmental activism around COP summits. These gatherings are not only places for policy discussions. They provide a platform for activists to push for action and direct criticism toward obstructive governments and corporations. Fossil of the Day as a strategic event Social movements take advantage of global events such as COP to name and shame political leaders or corporations that they identify as climate villains . At COP summits, the Climate Action Network hosts the Fossil of the Day award, as well as some other awards. The ceremony resembles a TV comedy sketch, where activists describe the key climate negotiation events they wish to highlight, and set out to embarrass those obstructing progress. While this is going on, a person in a dinosaur suit dances and music from Jurassic Park plays. Meanwhile, activists sing songs with lyrics they make up for the event. Fossil of the Day is about taking advantage of a critical event. Groups like the Climate Action Network award Fossils of the Day to try to affect media coverage, influence public opinion and ultimately pressure governments to take greater action to tackle climate change. Some critical events like COP happen on a regular schedule that is known in advance. We have referred to these as regularly scheduled critical events . Groups can plan ahead and take advantage of opportunities to comment on and critique the conversations going on in official spaces of deliberation among global leaders. Relatedly, interaction ritual theory explains phenomena that often occur in the context of a common action or event . Some key elements of the process include: group assembly (bodily co-presence), mutual focus of attention and shared mood. Engagement in interaction rituals often fosters group solidarity, emotional energy, symbols of social relationship and standards of morality. We can think about the Fossil of the Day in these terms. Activists and other COP participants routinely try to attend the Fossil of the Day award. It is an opportunity to meet up and rub elbows. Participants benefit from camaraderie, some light-hearted humour, and also, in some cases, righteous anger directed at leaders, governments and other bodies who obstruct climate action. These get-togethers reinforce social ties among the participants. Canada: Climate hero to climate villain? At COP21 in Paris, then-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau announced, “Canada is back!” The Trudeau government’s environment minister, Catherine McKenna, helped to negotiate the Paris Climate Agreement . One of Carney’s first acts as prime minister was to cancel the consumer carbon tax Trudeau brought in. And, among other things, Carney is now working to develop new oil and gas projects . At COP31, Carney was a no-show at the leaders summit. This past week, two former environment and climate change ministers criticized the record and direction of the current government. McKenna stated that the claim that Canada is still committed to its targets is “factually untrue.” Indeed, Canada consistently has one of the worst climate performance records . The Climate Change Performance Index, which compares the climate performance of 64 countries and the European Union, ranks Canada 62nd . This poor performance started before Carney’s tenure as prime minister , but Canada has been backsliding on the climate change file since he took office. In the view of many Canadians, Canada faces serious, and even existential, threats from the Trump-led United States. In the wake of this threat, Carney has been trying to boost economic growth and diversify international and domestic trade. Much of this has involved plans to grow the fossil fuel sector . articles.content: Prime Minister Mark Carney is riding a wave of domestic support and has emerged as the global poster child of a cautious but firm resistance to American bullies. He stood up to Donald Trump long before the recent Democratic landslide in the midterm elections in the United States. A central plank of Carney’s strategy consists of reducing Canada’s economic dependence on the U.S. by luring massive international investment to the country. Much of this investment into his “Projects of National Interest” will flow to infrastructure allowing Canada’s vast natural resources to access markets outside of North America. It would seem the midterm election results vindicate Carney. Yet, on closer inspection, things are more complicated. While Carney’s goal is commendable — a stable, sovereign Canada — the means he’s employing will arguably move Canada closer to the model of a society that is championed by … Donald Trump. Corporations benefit Consider the planned “mega tax deduction” designed to spur investment in pipelines, ports and extraction projects. The main beneficiaries would be multinational corporations and their shareholders, not Canadians. True, the investments would create jobs, but it’s worth noting that workers on both sides of the Canada-U.S. border have not received much of a share of growth in the last four decades. Other cases, such as the plan to privatize four large Canadian airports, are a classic short-term government cash grab . Compared to the Stellantis and Stelco debacles — when two major manufacturers failed to uphold job and production commitments made to Ottawa in exchange for federal backing or foreign-takeover approval — the federal government has a stronger position in the resource sector. That’s because the resources are located on Canadian soil. This opens up policy alternatives, which could include: Moving towards the Danish model of industrial foundations , where some profits are earmarked for social and environmental causes. Higher royalties from natural resource licences, which could be efficient in generating more for public coffers even if they marginally lowered private investment. Boosting the role of the Canada Infrastructure Bank to provide investment without loss of sovereignty, tied to Canada’s airports and ports. Eroding democratic norms In addition to the political substance, the Carney government’s efforts weaken democratic accountability. The omnibus Bill C-39 before Parliament weakens the rights of workers, non-governmental organizations and First Nations to contest the decisions made in the name of economic growth and “economic sovereignty.” Read more: What Bill C-39’s loosened environmental regulations could mean for Canadians Some First Nations probably feel the same way about Ottawa’s economic bulldozer strategy as Canadians feel about Trump’s actions. The Neskantaga First Nation’s battle to protect their homelands in northern Ontario is just one example. Sustainability Carney’s strategy is doubling down on the fossil fuel sector in Canada, too. This favours profit extraction and concentrated economic interests both at home and abroad over lower-income Canadians who are most likely to suffer from the consequences of climate change in terms of extreme weather, drought, wildfire and smoke. Once again, alternatives exist. Rather than export raw materials cheaply, why not invest in the processing of lumber, oil, gas, metals and minerals at home? For decades, part of Canada’s resource curse has been that most of the processing and economic value creation ( and job creation ) happens abroad, and Canadians pay dearly to purchase back the final products. Promoting forms of worker or producer co-operatives and vocational training programs would allow more evenly distributed forms of economic growth without increasing Canada’s carbon footprint. What’s more, investing in renewables has vast potential and is less prone to monopolizing profits. Read more: Fossil of the Day: Has Mark Carney made Canada a climate heretic? Carney’s amnesia? In sum, Carney’s Projects of National Interest look more like Projects of National Inequality and Environmental Destruction than measures that will promote Canada’s interests in a socially and environmentally sustainable fashion. Even without some of the more repulsive and narcissistic characteristics of Trump’s presidency, the economic policy outcome will be a country that is closer than ever before to Trump’s ideal for the U.S. The fact that someone as qualified and experienced as Carney falls into this trap is both surprising and to be expected at the same time. It’s surprising because Carney is well aware that policy measures have unintended, but foreseeable, negative consequences. In 2014, as governor of the Bank of England, he conceded that “the distributional consequences of the response to the financial crisis have been significant,” exacerbating inequality. He also founded the Network for Greening the Financial System in 2017, a group of central banks analyzing and guarding against the financial risks of climate change. In short, he sounded like a champion of sustainability. A striking case of amnesia about this former life seems to have befallen Carney since becoming prime minister. Yet it also has simple explanations. While corporate lobbyists in Ottawa may not be as powerful as they are in the U.S. capital, they clearly have substantial influence. In addition, Carney’s background as a banker predisposes him to favour financial interests over those of working Canadians when push comes to shove. What’s the point of fighting Trump when the price you pay is to import some elements of Trumpism to Canada? The consequences of Carney’s policy agenda, in terms of exacerbating the twin crises of economic inequality and environmental degradation, could be felt in Canada long after Trump has left the Oval Office. Peter Dietsch receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC) of Canada.

articles.content: Children with lifelong diseases and their families often seek answers about their illness from the internet. However, filtering out what is trustworthy information and what is not, and struggling to understand medical jargon, can leave children, teens and parents at risk of accepting unreliable information. That can be detrimental to care. Digital health literacy is the ability to find, evaluate and use electronic health information to help manage a health problem. People with higher levels of digital health literacy live healthier lives and make better health-related choices . To better understand how teens with chronic diseases and their caregivers navigate online health information, our pediatric rheumatology research team at the University of Saskatchewan spoke with adolescents living with chronic arthritis and related rheumatic diseases , along with their caregivers, to better understand how they access, evaluate and use online health information. The results from the interviews were recently published in the journal Children . While it wasn’t a surprise that all the teens and caregivers who were interviewed used the internet and technology for health support, as most Canadians do , there was considerable variability in how beneficial the information was for their health care. Information and misinformation Online health misinformation is widespread, and identifying what is trustworthy information can be difficult. Both adolescents and caregivers in our study said they often relied on common internet icons as indicators of the trustworthiness of online health information. These include the HTTPS padlock icon and the social media blue check mark. However, many did not realize that the padlock icon means secure data transfer and the check mark icon indicates a verified account, but neither symbol has any relevance to the reliability of the online health information. Read more: The vast majority of us have no idea what the padlock icon on our internet browser is – and it’s putting us at risk Adolescents and caregivers said they used online health information to answer “quick little questions,” as an alternative to “bothering” their health-care providers for an answer. Adolescents looked for online health information relating to how to manage symptoms and prepare for treatments, like dealing with a fear of needles. Caregivers looked for online health information to reassure themselves that their decisions about their child’s management are supported by reliable evidence and to reduce anxiety over their child’s health. However, both teens and caregivers reported they often can’t find the answers they’re looking for. This is because some of the answers don’t exist yet, such as the long-term effects of newer medications. Another problem identified was that online health information specifically for adolescents is limited. Most existing online health information is either geared toward younger children or is too complicated to understand. Role of medical teams As concerning as these findings are, the study found that the medical teams served as an important safety net for protecting patients and caregivers from misinformation. Most participants spoke of how they trust their medical teams. They described how they discuss online health information with their care providers before making health decisions. Read more: Online wellness content: 3 ways to tell evidence-based health information from pseudoscience The study showed that teens with rheumatic diseases and their caregivers confront barriers to developing high levels of digital health literacy while seeking online health information. These barriers include: An inability to confidently distinguish online health misinformation from reliable information, Eeliance on false indicators of online health information trustworthiness, and Misplaced trust in online health information by individuals inappropriately identifying as a medical doctor. Health-care providers, alongside children and teens with chronic diseases and their caregivers, should develop resources to support improving digital health literacy for patients and families and create online health information suitable for children, adolescents and their caregivers. Health-care teams should provide age-appropriate “prescriptions” that recommend strategies for accessing, interpreting and using reliable sources of online health information. Alan Rosenberg receives funding relevant to this project from the Canadian Rheumatology Association Foundation Craig Eling and Roona Sinha do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: Aging can seem like a negative process, one that causes our bodies to slow down and deteriorate. The aging brain, however, retains remarkable resilience. And some of the changes that occur within the aging brain are actually helpful adaptations. Our recent research study reveals this process of adaptation — showing that the brains of healthy older adults may cope better with lack of sleep than those of younger adults . Neuroplasticity in older age In this study, we investigated the neuroplasticity of human brain networks across the lifespan. Neuroplasticity refers to the brain’s extraordinary ability to change , particularly through the reorganization of brain connections. The most extreme periods of neuroplasticity occur during brain development in childhood , adolescence and the transition to early adulthood . However, the healthy brain retains its neuroplasticity throughout the lifespan, and undergoes periods of pronounced reorganization even in older age . Aging brains face many challenges, including cortical thinning or brain shrinkage , white matter demyelination and cognitive decline . As a result, many researchers treat aging as a proxy for purely negative brain changes. Our research goes against this trend by identifying multiple ways in which brain changes may actually be helpful adaptations to the challenges of aging. Preserving function for tomorrow Previous research has suggested that older adults do not suffer as badly from the negative effects of minimal sleep — decreased cognitive ability and mood — as younger adults do. In our study, we wanted to understand what is happening in the brain to cause this. So we compared the brains of younger adults (20-30 years) and older adults (65-75 years) after experiencing a full night of sleep and a night with only three hours of sleep. We found that part of the older brain’s functional connectivity responded in the opposite way to the brains of younger adults. After a night with only three hours of sleep, older adult brains reduced connections in a way that increased modularity . That is, their brain regions formed more local modules, with a small number of global connections between modules. Conversely, younger adult brains showed decreased modularity . Modularity is an efficient network organization associated with better cognitive outcomes . Our research suggests the brain may compensate for age-related changes by responding to short-term sleep loss in an adaptive way, preserving efficient brain function the next day. Strengthening local connections These findings complement our broader program of research identifying long-term reorganizations of brain networks that support cognitive outcomes in older age. Interestingly, these are distinct from the connectivity patterns that are beneficial for younger adults. We continue to see a recurring theme: The healthy brain seems to adapt to white matter demyelination with age by relying less on longer global connections and instead strengthening local connectivity . This growing program of research speaks to the healthy aging brain’s resilience to challenges, where neuroplasticity supports reorganization and adaptation. Sleep while you are young How do we help to promote these neuroplastic adaptations? One way is through physical activity . Another important lifestyle factor is getting a healthy amount of sleep throughout one’s life . Recent research has shown that sleep can directly affect both the risk of Alzheimer’s disease and how quickly it progresses . The amyloid and tau proteins that accumulate in brains with Alzheimer’s disease accumulate at a faster rate when sleep is disrupted . Researchers estimate that 15 per cent of Alzheimer’s disease cases could be prevented by identifying people with poor sleep quality and intervening to promote better sleep. The disease processes that cause Alzheimer’s disease develop for decades before an individual will experience memory loss and be diagnosed with dementia , so there is a large window of opportunity to detect and treat the disease and prevent cognitive decline. For some, sleep is an important treatment target. Brianne Kent receives funding from CIHR, NSERC, Canada Research Chairs, Michael Smith Health Research BC, and Canada Foundation for Innovation. Randy McIntosh receives funding from CIHR, NSERC, and CFI. articles.content: Climate change is a global reality, but people often encounter it through different local realities. For some, it enters everyday life through social media feeds, news reports, scientific findings and public discussion. For others, it is through water scarcity, food insecurity , floods , heatwaves, wildfires or the loss of a home or a loved one. Constant reports of climate impacts can leave people worn out. In a survey of 10,000 young people in 10 countries , more than half said they felt powerless and helpless about climate change. Climate news is also hard to follow and often emotionally draining , and about four in 10 people say they sometimes or often avoid the news. Communicators have assumed part of the problem is distance: that climate change feels far away in place and time . But a 2023 review of the research found most people already see it as current and close to home. The bigger gap may be in how we understand other people’s experiences of it. That is why climate communication needs to connect with the realities people live. Delegates from around the world are currently in Antalya, Turkey, for the COP31 climate summit . Up for discussion are major policy issues around climate finance, a just energy transition and adapting to climate change. But what can feel sidelined in these discussions are climate change’s impacts on the lives of people around the world. I am a PhD student in environmental engineering at the University of Northern British Columbia. I have lived, studied and worked in Africa, Europe and North America. Moving among places has shown me that people meet climate change from very different starting points. I see three ways that people come to understand climate change: by living through it, by learning about it and by relating it to a hardship of their own. I call these “paradigms of climate change experience.” They describe people who accept the evidence. They do not try to explain why some people reject it. Direct experience In late June 2021, a heatwave struck British Columbia. The town of Lytton recorded 49.6 C, Canada’s highest temperature on record . Scientists found the heatwave would have been “virtually impossible” without human-caused climate change. The BC Coroners Service linked 619 deaths to the heat. Most were older people, and many lived alone. For affected families, the meaning goes beyond statistics. It touches health, safety, income and the people they lost. Experiences like these can change how people see climate change. After the 2013-14 floods in the United Kingdom , people affected by flooding were more likely to see climate change as a personal threat. Indirect understanding People can imagine how serious a heat wave is without living through one. They can understand the danger of rising seas without living on a low-lying island. In November 2021, Tuvalu’s then-foreign minister, Simon Kofe, recorded his address to the COP26 climate conference while standing knee-deep in seawater, on land he said had once been dry. His presentation brought a small island state’s reality to audiences who would never otherwise experience it. People who understand climate change mainly by learning about it are not necessarily less concerned. Many might develop strong commitments through evidence and a sense of responsibility, without first suffering personally. Simon Kofe, then the foreign minister of Tuvalu, giving a recorded speech at COP26. Empathy grounded human experiences Someone may have never faced a heatwave, but still know what it means to lose a loved one. Someone with no experience of rising seas may still know what it is to be forced out of their homes. A family in British Columbia and a family in Tuvalu face different hazards. But each could recognize something of their own loss in the other’s story. This is my interpretation of how empathy might develop. Research suggests this kind of connection matters. People who feel compassion for others’ suffering are more willing to protect the environment. And climate messages told as personal stories have prompted more action than the same information presented as facts. The point is that people can recognize a shared human consequence without claiming an identical experience. Effective climate communication How to constructively communicate in the climate change era? Pair stories with science. Lived experience makes impacts real, but only attribution research can show what role climate change played. Focus on consequences, not hazards. The loss of a home, health or income is something most people can relate to, even when the cause differs. Let affected people speak for themselves. Kofe’s speech was effective because it came from someone living the reality. We should not have to experience every form of climate-related hardship before taking it seriously. Knowledge lets us understand beyond our own experience. Empathy gives us a reason to respond. Shagbaor Hycent Amool does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: Canada’s National Food Security Strategy aims to improve food security, affordability and to support locally grown and produced food. This 10-year, $3.2 billion strategy includes historic investments in domestic food production, processing and distribution. The strategy also recognizes that rural, remote and northern communities face distinct challenges that require targeted policy responses. But whether the strategy achieves its goals depends on how it’s implemented. As part of this strategy, the $1 billion federal Food-Link Fund was launched in October 2026. It consists of two programs: The Food Terminal Fund that supports large-scale wholesale food terminals, which are typically located in major urban centres and serve broad regional markets. The Food Hub Program , which aims to build storage, processing, aggregation and distribution infrastructure closer to producers that are typically located in smaller communities and rural regions. Rural considerations The two funding streams recognize that rural communities often face different transportation, distribution and infrastructure challenges and therefore require different supports. Evidence from other policy areas, like public transit and housing, shows that programs designed specifically for rural communities can be more effective. Read more: Is Canada finally investing in its rural communities? What funding for rural transit reveals The Common Ground Network released a research brief recommending ways to better understand the full range of services that Food Hubs provide to better position them for success within the National Food Security Strategy. Applying these recommendations to the Food-Link Fund can also help strengthen its impact in rural communities. The recommendations also reveal several potential challenges that policymakers should address. What does the Food-Link Fund get right? A “food hub” is a broad term that covers many community-based food activities . Past programs supporting food hubs often used narrow definitions of what counted as a food hub . In contrast, the Food-Link Fund focuses on desired outcomes. As described by the program guide : “Activities must be related to expanding and modernizing the existing network of food hubs and distribution systems to improve aggregation, processing, storage, and distribution options.” This flexibility allows communities to design projects that meet local needs. There are many local food security initiatives that already do these kinds of activities, even if they don’t call themselves food hubs. These include food co-operatives, solidarity supermarkets, independent grocers, farmers’ markets, food banks and other non-profit food distribution centres. The Food-Link Fund can support both new and existing initiatives, and allows applicants to build on what already exists. For-profits, non-profits and Indigenous organizations are all eligible to apply. Including non-profits is particularly important because many already play a key role in food distribution. The two-step application process may make it easier for organizations with less capacity to apply. If an expression of interest is approved, applicants have up to one year to prepare a full proposal. The fund also gives projects time to become stable and grow, offering up to $25 million per project over 10 years. This differs from many past programs that offered one-time funding and short timelines that have produced precarious conditions , making it harder for food hubs to maintain themselves and grow. What does the Food-Link Fund miss? Rural, remote and northern communities differ in terms of their size, accessibility and other place-specific traits. Needs and capacity can differ significantly. Unfortunately, some aspects of the Food-Link Fund are problematic for some rural places. The program’s desired outcomes include increased food distribution infrastructure, increased use of hubs by small and medium-sized businesses and stronger supply chains. But it pays less attention to social impacts and measures of success . For example, does food become more affordable or accessible? Are more people connected to health and social services? Do staff and volunteers gain valuable training and work experience? Is culturally appropriate food easier to access? Are local food systems better able to respond to disruptions? Read more: Canada’s new strategy won’t solve food insecurity or the health issues it creates Under the current program criteria, improvements in these areas don’t seem to count heavily in funding decisions. Yet food hubs are not simply places that move and store food. They also build relationships, trust and local capacity that help communities prevent and respond to crises. Financial sustainability is another key assessment criterion. Applicants must demonstrate that projects can continue operating without ongoing government support. While this may seem reasonable, it can disadvantage smaller and more remote communities where issues of accessibility and economies of scale mean the market economy is the least functional. Market failure can also be caused or made worse by poverty — impacting both rural and urban communities. Ironically, the communities facing market failures are often the same communities facing the greatest barriers to food access and distribution. These challenges are made worse by cost-sharing requirements. Applicants must secure 50 per cent of project costs, or 40 per cent for projects led by Indigenous or equity-deserving groups. Communities with the greatest financial needs are often the least able to provide matching funds. Securing matching funds The National Food Security Strategy recognizes that rural, remote and northern communities face unique food access challenges. Yet the Food-Link Fund’s emphasis on economic performance may create barriers precisely where needs are greatest. Some worthwhile projects may never reach the application stage because their goals are primarily social or because they cannot secure matching funds. As a result, the program may favour applicants or communities that are already well positioned to succeed rather than those facing the greatest food security challenges. Sarah-Patricia Breen receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada, the Province of British Columbia, ETSI-BC, and Mitacs. She is the past president of the Canadian Rural Revitalization Foundation. In her research she works closely with local partners, including the Kootenay Food Council. Jacob Kearey-Moreland is a researcher with the Common Ground Network, a project funded by the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC), in partnership with Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada (AAFC). He also serves as a volunteer board member with The Sharing Place Food Centre in Orillia, Ontario, Canada. Sara Edge is the Arrell Chair in Food, Policy & Society and receives funding from the Arrell Food Institute at the University of Guelph. She works with community partners that provide various food programs often through hub-based infrastructure.

articles.content: The latest episode of Saturday Night Live (SNL) featured a viral comedy sketch in which a series of men confidently explain that their sisters will shoulder the burden of caring for their aging parents. The sketch is funny because it’s so familiar. In just three minutes of satire, it captures a reality many women know all too well: when parents need care, daughters are often expected to step in while sons step aside. Social media reactions were swift. Responses ranged from “I am sister” to comments on social media calling on men to start doing their fair share. Beneath the humour lies an uncomfortable truth about who provides care and the growing pressures facing families as the population ages. The SNL sketch resonates because it reflects a private family reality that has become a public policy issue. The burden on women Globally, the International Labour Organization estimates 708 million women are unable to join the labour force because of unpaid care responsibilities . According to the United Nations, women around the world do 16 billion hours of unpaid care work every day. Cleaning, cooking and looking after the elderly are among the essential daily tasks predominantly performed by women and girls. In Canada, data show that women continue to shoulder most unpaid caregiving responsibilities . Men accounted for only 20 per cent of caregiving in the early 2000s, rising to 42 per cent by 2018. This progress is worth celebrating. As is the case globally, the Statistics Canada report also showed the intensity and type of the unpaid care remains highly gendered. Women are more likely to provide personal care, including bathing, dressing, feeding and toileting, while men are more likely to undertake home maintenance and outdoor work. Women also spend more time caregiving, averaging 10 hours a week compared with six hours for men. And this is happening at a time when several demographic forces are coming to a head. Globally, fertility rates are falling . More women are participating in the labour force around the world than ever before . Canada, for example, is experiencing its highest-ever rate of women aged 25-54 in the workforce, at 85 per cent . Taken together, these trends mean families are getting smaller and women are less available to serve as unpaid caregivers. Families therefore need to work together to make the division of labour between members more equitable. Women carers need to ask for the supports they need, and men need to step up, recognizing that care tasks, like cooking and medical management, are learned and can be taught. The role of the workplace But one of the most important places left to make the changes needed is the workplace. My research advocates for more carer-inclusive workplaces and caregiver-friendly employers. In Canada in 2018, one in 20 employees who were working full-time while also providing unpaid care to an adult left or intended to leave paid employment. Another one in seven worked fewer hours for pay. The consequences can be significant, particularly for women. Leaving a job or moving from full-time to part-time work can negatively affect health, income, pension, benefits, career progression, social networks and quality of life. Carer-friendly workplaces recognize that many of their employees are also managing unpaid care to an adult . These employers have policies and practices in place to support and accommodate employee-caregivers. These include flex time, telework, job sharing, paid or unpaid leave, government supports, benefits and caregiver support groups. Research shows there is a strong business case for these kinds of care-inclusive practices. A report from the American Association of Retired People found that for every dollar invested, employers can expect an average return of between two and four dollars. There are also increases in productivity, reduced absenteeism, lower presenteeism — when people are showing up to work but not really engaged — as well as improved employee retention and reduced recruitment costs. Supporting caregivers In Canada, provincial and jurisdictional supports are more readily available now than ever before, including those from the Ontario Caregivers Organization or the Family Caregivers of British Columbia . McMaster University in Hamilton, Ont., has partnered with the Canadian Standards Association to build a voluntary Carer-Inclusive and Accommodating Organizations Standard and handbook, “Helping worker-carers in your organization .” These tools will hopefully encourage workplaces across the country to better support employee-caregivers. Read more: Women caregivers need more support to manage their responsibilities and well-being The SNL sketch resonated because it transformed a familiar family tension into comedy. But for millions of women who are juggling both employment and an increasing unpaid care load, the issue is no laughing matter. Employers must recognize the ethical imperative and the business case for carer-inclusive workplace policies. This is critical as public health-care systems face increasing pressure, work lives grow busier and the population continues to age. Otherwise, we risk seeing more women burn out or leave the workforce altogether, undermining progress toward the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal of achieving gender equality . Allison Williams is a Tier 1 Canadian Research Chair in the Care Economy, Aging & Policy, funded by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research. The Partnership Research Program she leads is funded by the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC) and is entitled “The Care Economy, Aging and Policy: A Partnership Approach” (File Number: 895-2026-1023).

articles.content: A warning sign at Bartlett's Point Park in Corner Brook, NL. (Josie Wittmer) , CC BY The popular new Netflix thriller series Below portrays life in coastal Newfoundland and a frightening presence in the water that turns out to be a giant squid. However, the show’s tagline, “something’s in the water,” also speaks to another alarming reality in the water for many Newfoundland communities: sewage. Municipalities across the island of Newfoundland struggle to manage and dispose of raw sewage. The persistence of sewage effluent in local waters is experienced as a localized environmental threat, an infrastructural inequality, a burden on local finances and labour and a source of embarrassment in Newfoundland’s cities and towns that do not have the infrastructures to comply with federal wastewater management regulations. In a new SSHRC-funded project , I am exploring the mismatches between wastewater policies and local experiences of sewage infrastructure challenges in Newfoundland. Policy-infrastructure mismatches In Canada, wastewater is regulated at the federal level under the Fisheries Act by the Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations (WSER) . The regulations came into effect in 2015 and require secondary-level wastewater treatment (for example, facilities using biological processes to remove organic matter and suspended solids) to meet national quality standards and reduce threats to fish and human health. Yet, in Newfoundland and Labrador, 186 of 212 wastewater discharge points regulated by the WSER have no treatment at all . In 2021, only three per cent of Newfoundland and Labrador wastewater systems complied with the WSER . Map of Canada’s Effluent Quality results under the WSER (2021 results): Systems meeting WSER requirements at least 75 per cent of the time. (Generated by the author, November 2026) Under the WSER, non-compliant municipalities must apply for “transitional authorizations (TAs),” or permissions to continue polluting. TAs require regular sampling, analyses in authorized labs, acute-lethality (fish kill) tests and the submission of this data to a federal portal. However, many smaller communities with few municipal staff and small budgets struggle to finance, administer and monitor their water to meet these reporting requirements and continue polluting with permission. Infrastructural inequities Newfoundland communities of various sizes struggle to bridge the gap between the enforcement of federal environmental policies and their sewage management realities on the ground. For example, the City of Corner Brook releases over 20,000 square metres (approximately eight Olympic-sized swimming pools) of raw, untreated sewage effluent into the ocean every day. The city has struggled for more than a decade to obtain provincial and federal funds to build a secondary treatment facility. The estimated cost of the facility required in Corner Brook is $120-130 million . In early 2026, the city was served with an environmental directive by armed Department of Fisheries and Oceans officers who levied fines and threatened criminal charges because of the volume of effluent the city is releasing into the Bay of Islands. In the meantime, Corner Brook pays $60,000 a year to an authorized private lab to analyze their polluted water samples in order to provide the required data to the federal government’s portal. Small communities across the island are also dealing with big sewage issues. In addition to lacking wastewater treatment facilities, many municipalities have aging sewage infrastructure and experience frequent sewage blockages, line breaks and overflow. For small towns with an increased population during warmer months due to seasonal residents, workers and tourists, these challenges compound as the sewage increases. The town clerk of a community with around 1,000 residents recently estimated that 30 per cent of the town’s budget could be spent elsewhere if not for the costs of water and sewage infrastructure repairs and wastewater monitoring . Contracting out wastewater sampling For many small municipalities, producing data to keep a transitional authorization can be a labour burden, logistically challenging and expensive. Third-party companies are stepping in to fill the gap between regulations and municipal realities by selling wastewater sampling, lab and consulting services for a fee. In a recent interview, an elected official in a small western Newfoundland town with a population of less than 500 residents told me: “When you see the (company) van drive through town, you know there’s also an $8,000 invoice coming.” A 2019 report in The Telegram estimated that 80 per cent of Newfoundland municipalities contract out their wastewater sampling and analysis to one firm , Biomaxx Environmental. Following global trends in wastewater monitoring and the growing presence of private sector solutions for municipal wastewater challenges , I suggest the current enforcement of WSER is creating the conditions for community wastewater challenges to become a source of profit. In other words, wastewater is emerging as a place where private companies are creating a market for themselves in municipalities struggling to comply with regulations that were not made with their infrastructure realities in mind. ‘Get back from the water’ In Below , Josh Hartnett’s Calvin Penney runs through a community event shouting for everyone to “get back from the water!” When watching the scene, I was reminded of stories I’ve heard from municipal staff and residents of Newfoundland communities running up to tourists to tell them to stay out of the waters near outfalls, where pipes, drains or sewers discharge wastewater into bodies of water. One such incident included a cruise ship passenger clad in snorkel equipment, wading into the waters from the beach directly in front of Corner Brook’s largest sewage outfall. Untreated sewage — along with the disconnect between federal regulations and local infrastructure — is a major obstacle in communities that still lack wastewater treatment. Local sewage challenges also reach far beyond environmental pollution and municipal budgets, affecting community planning, tourism, public health, recreation, local food sovereignty and access to shoreline food sources. articles.description: A warning sign at Bartlett's Point Park in Corner Brook, NL. (Josie Wittmer) , CC BY The popular new Netflix thriller series Below portrays life in coastal Newfoundland and a frightening presence in the water that turns out to be a giant squid. However, the show’s tagline, “something’s in the water,” also speaks to another alarming reality in the water for many Newfoundland communities: sewage. Municipalities across the island of Newfoundland struggle to manage and dispose of raw sewage. The persistence of sewage effluent in local waters is experienced as a localized environmental threat, an infrastructural inequality, a burden on local finances and labour and a source of embarrassment in Newfoundland’s cities and towns that do not have the infrastructures to comply with federal wastewater management regulations. In a new SSHRC-funded project , I am exploring the mismatches between wastewater policies and local experiences of sewage infrastructure challenges in Newfoundland. Policy-infrastructure mismatches In Canada, wastewater is regulated at the federal level under the Fisheries Act by the Wastewater Systems Effluent Regulations (WSER) . The regulations came into effect in 2015 and require secondary-level wastewater treatment (for example, facilities using biological processes to remove organic matter and suspended solids) to meet national quality standards and reduce threats to fish and human health. Yet, in Newfoundland and Labrador, 186 of 212 wastewater discharge points regulated by the WSER have no treatment at all . In 2021, only three per cent of Newfoundland and Labrador wastewater systems complied with the WSER . articles.content: Liberal members of Parliament in Canada recently agreed to amend the controversial proposed legislation, Bill C-39 , that critics say would undermine environmental protections and Indigenous and labour rights if passed into law. The amendments come days after protests against the bill took place in cities across Canada. The proposed legislation, called the Building Canada Strong Act, aims to fast-track development projects such as pipelines and mines. In line with that push, the Canadian government recently turned its attention to reviving interest in Arctic offshore oil and gas. The fall 2026 budget earmarked millions of dollars for northern oil and gas governance . Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced plans for consultations and capacity-building in the western Arctic, with an eye toward lifting a federal moratorium on offshore oil and gas extraction in the Canadian Arctic . But will this surge of political support lead to hydrocarbon production in the region? Arctic oil and gas moratorium In 2016, the Canadian and American governments implemented a moratorium on Arctic drilling . The ban was meant to support climate commitments, study the environmental risks and develop parks and protected areas in line with international commitments to preserve lands and waters . The ban’s ultimate promise was to build a sustainable Arctic economy , in partnership with other Arctic nations. But its reception in the North was mixed. Concern about missed potential economic opportunities came with concern from others that the ban didn’t go far enough . A CBC News report on the Canadian government reviewing the Arctic oil and gas drilling ban. Bill C-39 has been criticized for the potential limits it would place on environmental protections, Indigenous and labour rights in the name of “ building Canada strong .” Arctic oil and gas opportunities appear to be one of the target resources of this policy. The history of Arctic offshore oil and gas extraction in Canada can tell us a lot about how these proposals might take shape in the present and future. The history of Canada’s attempt to build an oil and gas economy in Arctic waters is, for the most part, a history of failed projects. Expensive, complex and risky Why did Arctic oil and gas projects fail? The most obvious answer is a combination of climate, geography and the risks these projects produce. In short, it is hugely expensive, technically complex and ecologically risky to move oil and gas from Arctic waters to southern refineries and markets. Uncertainty around jurisdiction and local community benefits further complicates the question of Arctic oil and gas . On a broader scale, interest in offshore hydrocarbon resources in Arctic Canada tends to wax and wane alongside shifting geopolitical tensions and instabilities in oil-producing regions globally. The Berger Inquiry into the Mackenzie Valley pipeline unfolded in the shadow of the 1973 oil embargo and Arab-Israeli War. The 1979 Iranian Revolution and oil shocks reinvigorated pressure for Arctic oil and gas production, with several Canadian and international energy companies submitting proposals for offshore production in the Beaufort Sea . A revived proposal for a natural gas pipeline in the Mackenzie Valley was assessed in the context of surging energy prices tied to the 2003 invasion of Iraq by the United States. In each case, global prices for oil and gas dropped before the proposed projects began, rendering production commercially unviable. Science fiction infrastructure dreams This geopolitical intrigue has made Arctic offshore oil and gas into a “stranded resource” — it’s easy to see the appeal of an untapped reserve. To solve the Arctic oil and gas riddle, engineers and oil executives have dreamed up a dizzying array of technological adaptations and infrastructures to move oil and gas to southern markets. Drill rigs on floating ice islands of sand dredged from the ocean floor. Oil tankers split in half and towed into the Beaufort Sea. A type of 12-propeller plane, nicknamed the Brute Lifter , ferrying oil to Edmonton in the fuselage. Nuclear submarines full of oil sailing under the ice. Arctic island-hopping gas pipelines . These and more science-fictional infrastructure dreams were all in the mix at one point or another. Similar ideas will have to be brought into being if the Canadian government proceeds with further exploration of Arctic oil and gas. Arctic resources as crisis response The current push has many of the hallmarks of previous attempts to drill in Arctic waters. Carney’s interest in lifting the federal moratorium on offshore oil and gas extraction similarly responds to geopolitical instability and proposes huge, “dreamy” infrastructure investment. In this case, the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran are driving Canadian politicians to once again look to Arctic hydrocarbons as a crisis response . Projects of “ national interest ” — such as an invigorated oil and gas economy in the western Arctic and Beaufort Sea or the Port of Churchill Plus in northern Manitoba — are likely to gain traction. Time, money and work will be invested into consultations and assessments, including significant resources and labour from Indigenous organizations and communities. The issue will likely once again prove divisive within and between Indigenous communities and organizations, leading to political conflict over proposed exploration and extraction activities. The end result is likely to be the same as previous attempts to extract oil and gas from Arctic waters in Canada. Projects will face the usual insurmountable economic, environmental and political barriers to development, and interest in Arctic oil and gas will once again wane. The last well drilled in the Beaufort Sea was in 2006. It remains to be seen if the Carney government can surmount the social, environmental and geopolitical barriers that led to previous failures to build an oil and gas economy in Canada’s Arctic. Jonathan Peyton receives funding from SSHRC. Warren Bernauer receives funding from the Canada Research Chair Program.

articles.content: A new day, a new cyberattack. The most recent is an attack that impacted 178 major websites, including those of the BBC, CNN, Zoom, HSBC, Salesforce and Equifax . This follows a series of cyberattacks and disruptions over the last two months — most notably on supermarkets throughout Europe. A series of attacks in France during October raised refrigerator and freezer temperatures to 50 C in more than 350 supermarkets. Overnight, large amounts of food spoiled, equipment overheated and fires were reported. Affected stores had to discard food and temporarily close. Similar attacks and disruptions were then reported across several countries in November, including Ireland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Estonia, Finland and Luxembourg. In all of these cases, hackers remotely reprogrammed internet-connected temperature controls. They switched evaporators to defrost mode, raising temperatures beyond safety limits. These simple changes impacted physical equipment, businesses and people. How will the next cyberattack unfold, and where? Our industrial critical infrastructure offers many targets — from blood banks to chemical manufacturing plants , nuclear reactors , aviation and other transportation systems and wastewater treatment facilities . The potential consequences are vast. Our team at the Cyber Security Evaluation and Assurance (CyberSEA) research lab at Carleton University has simulated cyberattacks on a Canadian municipal wastewater treatment facility to identify the most serious consequences. We have also mapped out seven dimensions for understanding cyberattack impacts . The vulnerability of critical infrastructure Critical infrastructure refers to 10 broad sectors including energy and utilities, water, health, transportation and food. Systems in these sectors provide essential services. Connecting the systems to the internet improves efficiency, but can also expose such services to modern cybersecurity threats. Cybersecurity analysis tends to focus on attacks and how they could have been prevented. Cyberattack impact analysis , on the other hand, looks at what happens after a system is compromised — which operations are disrupted, how the effects spread and who or what might be harmed. A supermarket is more than its refrigerator temperature controls. It’s a system involving food, equipment, employees, customers, business continuity and public confidence. Similarly, a water utility contains pumps and software but also protects a wider system of treatment processes, public health, the environment and access to safe water. Cyberattacks on critical infrastructure radiate impact through all of our lives. Learning from wastewater systems Wastewater treatment provides a good example of the far-reaching consequences of a cyberattack. When we simulated cyberattacks on a Canadian municipal wastewater treatment facility , we found this could force equipment to operate excessively or near safety limits. It could also increase chemical consumption, push the plant into costly contingency modes or interfere with chemical dosing. The most serious scenario involved discharging under-treated wastewater into the city’s river. This might seem extreme, but something similar has already happened. In 2000, a former employee attacked the Maroochy Shire wastewater system in Australia . He remotely interfered with sewage pumping stations, preventing pumps and alarms from operating properly. Over three months, millions of gallons of untreated sewage entered waterways and local parks. 7 dimensions of impact Our recent research identifies seven dimensions for understanding the consequences of cyberattacks. The supermarket attacks across Europe illustrate all seven. Operational impacts occur when a system cannot perform its intended function, while physical impacts involve changes or damage to equipment and materials. In the supermarkets, altered temperature controls disrupted food preservation, equipment overheated and food spoiled. The consequences can then spread beyond the system. Safety impacts expose people to hazards, such as fires or unsafe food. Environmental impacts harm air, water, land or ecosystems — such as discarded food creating additional waste. Economic impacts include lost products, equipment repairs, downtime and lost customers. Broader consequences may also emerge. Societal impacts disrupt communities or their access to important goods and services, such as fresh food. Reputational impacts arise when people lose confidence in an organization or service, for example, due to concerns about food safety. These dimensions are connected. One disrupted operation can produce several impacts at once, some continuing after the technical problem has been resolved. Preparing for consequences We may not know how the next cyberattack will unfold. But we can prepare for unsafe water, damaged equipment, environmental harm, interrupted services, financial losses and diminished public trust. Impact analysis helps decision-makers ask practical questions: Which consequences are unacceptable? Where are additional safeguards needed? Who must respond when safety or environmental harm occurs? Which services must be restored first? The goal is not merely to keep attackers out of computer systems. It is to keep essential services working when cyber-defences fail. Jason Jaskolka receives funding from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC). He is affiliated with the Rogers Cybersecure Catalyst as an Academic Fellow (2026-2027). articles.content: Ontario Education Minister Paul Calandra recently discussed concerns about whether Ontario’s “inclusion model” in education was working . The comments were made after a social policy committee hearing where the minister was asked about gaps in funding special education needs . Concerns about inclusion models are in the news elsewhere too. But researchers note a lack of agreement around what inclusion means and importantly , what it implies for education policy and student services . In Ontario, depending on who you ask, the discussion around an “inclusion model” and its success or failure could involve the increased reports of violence in the classroom , funds to support students with exceptionalities , class size, educator resources , student attendance or other important topics. More clarity is needed in Ontario around what we mean by models of inclusive education in terms of where, how and what students learn. Where, how, what students learn Researchers note that the essential element of a model is its usefulness for a specific purpose. For example, the map of my university helps new students find their way from one building to another, but it’s not useful for finding the coziest study spots. A map or model of inclusive education would provide clear guidelines of what this is, and what it isn’t, and what should be expected in the education of students with exceptionalities. While Ontario has standards and definitions that address specialized supports for students with exceptionalities, currently, decisions for the 360,000-plus students with special needs are made on a case-by-case basis. A clear model could mean more guidance from the province and collective agreement on expectations for educational decisions. What guides inclusive education? Inclusive Education Canada emphasizes student belonging and value with a focus on meaningful engagement of students with disabilities “alongside their peers without disabilities.” UNESCO describes a model of inclusive education that guides “equitable access to quality learning.” It envisions a focus on educator collaboration, flexible and individualized curricula and supports in unified learning environments. Federally, Canada has committed to the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities . This includes a pledge to promote access to support in general education environments enabled by appropriate teacher training. In Ontario, the Education Act’s Regulation 181/98 , pertaining to “Identification and placement of exceptional pupils,” assumes children should be placed in a general education class with appropriate supports before considering specialized placement options. The provincial Ministry of Education’s Policy/Program Memorandum 119 defines inclusive education as being: “Based on the principles of acceptance and inclusion of all students. Students see themselves reflected in their curriculum, their physical surroundings and the broader environment.” Special education policy in Ontario requires boards to make note of their special education “service-delivery model” for students with exceptionalities, within their ministry-reviewed annual special education plans . However, the requirement doesn’t ask boards how services for students relate to fostering inclusion. Inclusion models have evolved Over time, inclusion models in general have evolved . The focus shifted from where students learn (from special education to general education classrooms) to where and how students learn. This change has involved adding specialized and inclusive teaching strategies in general classroom settings. Current models combine a focus on where, how and what students learn. “What” implies robust academic expectations and sufficient support for academic achievement. Ontario decisions about where students learn — termed “educational placement decisions” — are made by the Identification, Placement, and Review Committees . These include at least three members (for example: a school principal, students 16 years or older, a student’s parents and other relevant school staff). Research from my colleagues and me shows that educational placement in general settings has increased over time, but not for all students. Students with behavioural exceptionalities did not see increased placements in inclusive settings. Students identified with developmental disabilities or who are deaf or hard of hearing had some increased placements in general classrooms, but still had the lowest placements there. Researchers have documented the subjective and contextual nature of such decisions. Like other researchers , we also found that external factors , including school board and student age, were significant predictors of educational placement decisions. Read more: Navigating special education labels is complex, and it matters for education equity How students learn: support decisions Ontario’s Learning for All policy promoted general inclusive strategies such as Universal Design for Learning and Differentiated Instruction. But support decisions are made by a student’s educators and recorded and tracked in the student’s Individual Education Plan (IEP). Ontario’s latest audit report and research on teacher training in the province point to problems in teacher education, as well as resources and practices that can negatively influence developing IEPs and ultimately student learning supports. Read more: Children on individual education plans: What parents need to know, and 4 questions they should ask What students learn The Ontario curriculum is designed to describe essential learning expectations for knowledge and skills for all students across the province. Students with special education needs may receive supports accessing the curriculum through educational accommodations. These increase support but don’t change the learning expectation. However, some students with disabilities access the curriculum in a modified format: learning expectations are simplified. Modifications can be helpful to identify learning gaps and provide high-intensity supports. However, there are concerns that this approach is overused, as noted in the Ontario Human Rights Commission’s Right to Read inquiry report . Beyond curricular modification, students with exceptionalities may also participate in alternate programs, addressing, for example, life skills. Similar to placement and supports, educational content access is determined on a case-by-case basis for students with special education. For some students, like those with a learning disability, mild intellectual disability or developmental disability, assumptions about difficulties learning academic content are set in the identification definitions themselves. What do we want inclusive model to be? Without clear consensus on what inclusive education means and what the model in Ontario refers to, debate around its success is a bit like arguing over who makes the authentic version of an unwritten family recipe. What’s really needed, instead, is to ask: What do we want this model to be? To enact and evaluate change to increase successful outcomes for students, we need to think about what we value in terms of the where, what and how of education, for the approximately 16 per cent of the Ontario student population with special education needs. In Ontario, depending on who you ask, the discussion around an “inclusion model” and its success or failure could involve the increased reports of violence in the classroom , funds to support students with exceptionalities , class size, educator resources , student attendance or other important topics. More clarity is needed in Ontario around what we mean by models of inclusive education in terms of where, how and what students learn. Where, how, what students learn Researchers note that the essential element of a model is its usefulness for a specific purpose. For example, the map of my university helps new students find their way from one building to another, but it’s not useful for finding the coziest study spots. A map or model of inclusive education would provide clear guidelines of what this is, and what it isn’t, and what should be expected in the education of students with exceptionalities. While Ontario has standards and definitions that address specialized supports for students with exceptionalities, currently, decisions for the 360,000-plus students with special needs are made on a case-by-case basis. A clear model could mean more guidance from the province and collective agreement on expectations for educational decisions. What guides inclusive education? Inclusive Education Canada emphasizes student belonging and value with a focus on meaningful engagement of students with disabilities “alongside their peers without disabilities.” UNESCO describes a model of inclusive education that guides “equitable access to quality learning.” It envisions a focus on educator collaboration, flexible and individualized curricula and supports in unified learning environments. Federally, Canada has committed to the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities . This includes a pledge to promote access to support in general education environments enabled by appropriate teacher training. In Ontario, the Education Act’s Regulation 181/98 , pertaining to “Identification and placement of exceptional pupils,” assumes children should be placed in a general education class with appropriate supports before considering specialized placement options. The provincial Ministry of Education’s Policy/Program Memorandum 119 defines inclusive education as being: “Based on the principles of acceptance and inclusion of all students. Students see themselves reflected in their curriculum, their physical surroundings and the broader environment.” Special education policy in Ontario requires boards to make note of their special education “service-delivery model” for students with exceptionalities, within their ministry-reviewed annual special education plans . However, the requirement doesn’t ask boards how services for students relate to fostering inclusion. Inclusion models have evolved Over time, inclusion models in general have evolved . The focus shifted from where students learn (from special education to general education classrooms) to where and how students learn. This change has involved adding specialized and inclusive teaching strategies in general classroom settings. Current models combine a focus on where, how and what students learn. “What” implies robust academic expectations and sufficient support for academic achievement. Ontario decisions about where students learn — termed “educational placement decisions” — are made by the Identification, Placement, and Review Committees . These include at least three members (for example: a school principal, students 16 years or older, a student’s parents and other relevant school staff). Research from my colleagues and me shows that educational placement in general settings has increased over time, but not for all students. Students with behavioural exceptionalities did not see increased placements in inclusive settings. Students identified with developmental disabilities or who are deaf or hard of hearing had some increased placements in general classrooms, but still had the lowest placements there. Researchers have documented the subjective and contextual nature of such decisions. Like other researchers , we also found that external factors , including school board and student age, were significant predictors of educational placement decisions. Read more: Navigating special education labels is complex, and it matters for education equity How students learn: support decisions Ontario’s Learning for All policy promoted general inclusive strategies such as Universal Design for Learning and Differentiated Instruction. But support decisions are made by a student’s educators and recorded and tracked in the student’s Individual Education Plan (IEP). Ontario’s latest audit report and research on teacher training in the province point to problems in teacher education, as well as resources and practices that can negatively influence developing IEPs and ultimately student learning supports. Read more: Children on individual education plans: What parents need to know, and 4 questions they should ask What students learn The Ontario curriculum is designed to describe essential learning expectations for knowledge and skills for all students across the province. Students with special education needs may receive supports accessing the curriculum through educational accommodations. These increase support but don’t change the learning expectation. However, some students with disabilities access the curriculum in a modified format: learning expectations are simplified. Modifications can be helpful to identify learning gaps and provide high-intensity supports. However, there are concerns that this approach is overused, as noted in the Ontario Human Rights Commission’s Right to Read inquiry report . Beyond curricular modification, students with exceptionalities may also participate in alternate programs, addressing, for example, life skills. Similar to placement and supports, educational content access is determined on a case-by-case basis for students with special education. For some students, like those with a learning disability, mild intellectual disability or developmental disability, assumptions about difficulties learning academic content are set in the identification definitions themselves. What do we want inclusive model to be? Without clear consensus on what inclusive education means and what the model in Ontario refers to, debate around its success is a bit like arguing over who makes the authentic version of an unwritten family recipe. What’s really needed, instead, is to ask: What do we want this model to be? To enact and evaluate change to increase successful outcomes for students, we need to think about what we value in terms of the where, what and how of education, for the approximately 16 per cent of the Ontario student population with special education needs. articles.title: For better inclusive education that really supports students, we need to consider what we value

articles.content: Editor’s note: This story is part of a series of articles from Canada’s top social sciences and humanities academics in a partnership between the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and The Conversation Canada. Back in 2008, every other week during the school year, my research team (six students in Concordia University’s Design and Computation Arts department as well as two research associates in my lab) and I made the 20-minute drive from Montréal to the Kahnawake Survival School . We’d been invited by Owisokon Lahache, a Kahnawake Mohawk artist and arts teacher. Our goal was to prototype a new model for teaching Indigenous teenagers digital production skills within the context of their community’s history, language and culture. What we learned there changed how I thought about research itself. We spent that fall immersed in storytelling and discussing the importance of those stories to the community. In the winter, we focused on teaching the students tools and techniques for making video games — storyboarding, concept art, modelling, animation and programming. In March, we asked them to use what they had learned to design a video game themselves. We weren’t sure what the students would come up with, and were particularly curious about whether the students would be able to translate oral storytelling into an interactive video game. When we returned to their classroom, we were astounded. Spread across four desks was white butcher paper with a complete game level designed in pencil and clay. The students had taken a monster from one story, a landscape from another and a conflict from a third and remixed them into a new narrative without our guidance. It was then that we realized how excited they had been to be asked to tell their community’s stories in their own way. The students understood video games and had no problem designing one whose world, characters and internal logic were rooted in their own knowledge systems and territory. That experience — a combination of tradition, technology and preparing Indigenous youth for fluency in the digital storytelling tools of the future — became a major driver behind the creation of the Initiative for Indigenous Futures (IIF) . Flipping the research relationship IIF was a partnership of universities and community organizations in Canada, funded by a Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC) Partnership Grant (as well as a Trudeau Fellowship) running from 2015 to 2022. Over seven years, IIF worked with people from numerous communities across Canada, the U.S. and the Pacific, including Kanien’kehá:ka, Cree, Anishinaabe, Diné, Métis, Mi'kmaq, Kānaka Maoli and Māori. We invited experts from many domains — fine arts, design, computer science, history, language — to join us, and we relied on our shared passion to establish methodologies that allowed us to work across communities and disciplines. At its core was a concept called the Indigenous Future Imaginary : the idea that Indigenous Peoples must first imagine the futures we want before we can build our way toward them — that the visions communities hold of their tomorrows shape the work they do today. Developing those imagined futures required spaces for Indigenous communities to dream, cultural grounding to maintain continuity, freedom to speculate creatively and technical capacity to help turn those visions into reality. IIF was designed to provide all four. The partnership model IIF developed was a deliberate departure from how academic research typically works . Often, universities set the questions, communities provide access or data and outcomes circulate within institutions the communities rarely encounter. IIF inverted this. Community members developed their own future imaginaries, with IIF providing support and encouragement, and research questions were developed in response: What are Kanien'kehá:ka values? What does a video game look like when it’s designed to carry them? What creative and technical infrastructure do Indigenous artists need to visualize futures and sustain a practice over time? That inversion took shape through four interconnected pillars: workshops that built technical capacity; residencies supporting artists’ deep engagement with the technology, along with commissions to help populate the future with Indigenous images; symposia and lecture series that circulated these methods more widely; and preservation of digital media artworks for future generations. Skins Workshops on Aboriginal Storytelling in Digital Media , one of IIF’s main initiatives, is now in its 18th year, after 120 workshops reaching more than 1,500 participants across communities from Canada to Hawai'i to Aotearoa to Finland. Another IIF initiative led to Abundant Intelligences , the $28 million international research collaboration exploring how to integrate AI into Indigenous knowledge systems. Collaborations generate grounded outcomes The Initiative for Indigenous Futures model carries lessons well beyond Indigenous research contexts for the scholars who design studies, the institutions that house them and the funders who pay for them. For scholars, investing time in the communities where you’ve built research establishes a foundation of trust that makes it possible to do work that is generative for them and you. Read more: Canada’s first Inuit-led university is coming to Nunavut — here’s why it matters For academic institutions, shared intellectual leadership provides sustained knowledge production where different problems have time to come into view and be addressed. It creates the space for epistemological breadth that enriches our understanding of innovative ways of engaging with our world. For funders, it means that research impact looks different when it is shaped with and for community. Workshops, artworks, games and technical capacity built over years are not soft outputs alongside the “real” academic work. They are the real work. When more communities are given the tools, the space and the institutional trust to imagine their futures on their own terms, the futures we collectively arrive at are richer, more honest and better equipped to hold the full complexity of what it means to live in the world. Jason Edward Lewis receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, the Canadian Fund for Innovation, the New Frontiers of Research Fund, the MacArthur Foundation, and the Schmidt Family Foundation.
