I am a Registered Professional Planner who specialized in environmental planning during graduate school. My work over the past 20 years, though, has often been more about what land can be used for and how it’s used. Marineland has been around since the 1960s. Its record of bad things happening to animals only grew over time . I can now see how the mistreatment of the whales and dolphins was inevitable. The orientation of planning Planning has been a formal occupation in Canada since 1919 . It has the legal status of a self-regulating profession now. Planners often work for governments, especially municipalities. Personally, I’ve analyzed land-use plans as a consultant. In my work for a provincial government, I’ve told other planners what needs to change before a plan or its implementing bylaw can be approved. And as a municipal planner, I’ve made decisions about how humans can use land. The City of Niagara Falls’ Official Plan describes Marineland as “family entertainment.” No words in this legal planning document speak to the conditions the sea mammals needed to survive, let alone thrive. Yet it’s the document that legitimized Marineland’s existence. The nails in the coffins A February 2025 Committee of Adjustment meeting haunts me. Committees of Adjustment are a sub-structure of municipal governments in Ontario. They are allowed under Section 44 of the provincial government’s Planning Act . Committees of Adjustment make decisions about proposed changes to land that are minor, and that also don’t meet the requirements in municipal planning documents. Since these committees are a planning mechanism, planning staff help them do their work. The Niagara Falls committee considered eight different applications about Marineland in February 2025. Each was approved . Together, they brought Marineland into compliance with the city’s Official Plan and Zoning Bylaw. Niagara Falls adopted a new Official Plan in August 2026, which is still awaiting approval from the provincial government. Many wheels need to be set in motion before an actual application to eventually redevelop land materializes. This was one of those wheels. After the February 2025 meeting, Marineland applied for federal approval to export the whales and dolphins (which was at first denied), then said that it would euthanize them (more than once) and finally received federal approval to export them. Hierarchies of power and public processes The planning process can be the only public opportunity to point out something that could, otherwise, go unnoticed. At the February 2025 meeting, people expressed concerns about what would happen to Marineland’s whales and dolphins. Some attendees asked the committee to defer its decision until there was more information about how the animals on the site would be treated. Marineland’s representative suggested that the approvals they sought were unrelated to animal welfare . Marineland had asked for variances, easements, new parcel creation and mortgage release to secure operational financing. The municipality’s planners had evaluated the applications as minor, based on how there was no actual development being proposed, how no neighbouring properties would be impacted and how streetscape and character wouldn’t be compromised. If it sounds like jargon, that’s because it is. Over time, planning has become a profession with its own language and processes. Often, when I’m talking to a non-planner, I’m simply translating. The planning priorities in the jargon are not unusual either. Mechanisms like Committees of Adjustment have also been called out for reducing greater public participation . Finding a better way Peekachu, Rain, Osiris, Caspian, Jellybean, Cyprus and Echo didn’t fit into the planning process. Sweden-based planning theorist Jonathan Metzger calls the effect “radical exclusion.” As a practitioner who has turned to a PhD, I’m painfully aware that planners think not in terms of life, but land. The Canadian planning profession’s most recent update to its ethical standards doesn’t do animals justice either. Marineland’s tanks and enclosures may be empty now. Fur farms, factory farms, testing labs and zoos still stand. The path to different futures is not easy. Animals are legally property. So is land. There is urgency, though, and a need for answers that are kinder than the status quo. In their new book , Animals and The Right to Politics , philosophy scholars Sue Donaldson and Will Kymlicka imagine a city with two distinct governance systems. In addition to the existing municipal government, they propose a new political entity that takes over land and development decisions. The intention is to create a more stable, peaceful world for animals. Plausible or not, we must move towards some new normal. Humanity is a hollow word if we don’t. But I don’t see it happening unless non-planners insist that planning work consider every sentient being, not just humans. Pooja Kumar received the Ontario Graduate Scholarship (2026-2027) to generally support her PhD studies. She is a Member of the Canadian Institute of Planners and the Prince Edward Island Institute of Professional Planners. She became a Registered Professional Planner in 2010, with the Ontario Professional Planners Institute.
articles.title: Was a kinder fate possible for Marineland’s animals? How the planning process failed them

articles.content: Sighting a humpback whale from a boat can be awe-inspiring. For some BC Ferries passengers, that experience became disturbing when their ferry struck and fatally injured a humpback whale on Oct. 18. The whale was later identified as BCX1700 , nicknamed Notcho. Notcho’s death, and the ceremony Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw (Squamish Nation) held to honour him, made national news . Coverage of Notcho’s death may elicit feelings of anger, sadness or despair. These are forms of what is called ecological grief : the emotional response caused by experiencing or learning about environmental destruction, species extinction, biodiversity loss and climate change. Effective ways to cope with ecological grief depend on the situation and the person . A common suggestion for people feeling ecological grief is to take action. In Notcho’s case, the Marine Education and Research Society provided practical solutions for preventing future ship strikes based on the details of his death. Online responses from members of the public to the Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw ceremony show that mourning practices can also be helpful for coping. Notcho’s story North Pacific humpback whales are a conservation success story in many ways. Their populations have been recovering since they were legally protected from commercial whaling in 1966. Unfortunately, as their numbers in the Salish Sea increase, so does the risk of ship strikes . The same behaviour that allows people to enjoy them — spending time at the surface feeding or resting — also puts them at risk of collisions with boats. Fatal ship strikes of whales are not unusual, and there are specific reasons Notcho’s death became a national news story: his fatal injury was preventable, traumatic and witnessed up close by several people. He had a name and had been known in the area for almost 10 years. Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw recognized Notcho as a relative and honoured him accordingly . Ecological grief is normal and healthy Ecological grief can be experienced in relation to many types of ecological losses , such as individual animals like Notcho, cherished trees like the Golden Spruce or entire species and ecosystems, to name just a few. It can also be felt in response to the impacts of climate change . Researchers, and the public more broadly, increasingly understand ecological grief as a healthy and valid emotional response . As with any form of grief, mourning is a beneficial, and even necessary, process for coping with emotions. Ecological grief itself has been well-studied and described, but effective ways of coping with it, and of mourning ecological losses, are not as well understood . Coping with ecological losses I have spent my career working in conservation biology, and this is not my first brush with ecological grief. It’s an unfortunate occupational hazard . I recently returned to academia to investigate strategies for coping with it. Through my preliminary research, I have been exploring three forms of coping : action-focused (or problem-solving), emotion-focused and meaning-focused. When I heard the news about Notcho and went online for more information, I noticed evidence of all three in public reactions to a post made by Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw on their Facebook page about an honouring ceremony for Notcho. On Facebook, members of the public expressed action-focused reactions when they conveyed frustration about ferry speed limits in the area and called for changes. Some people wanted to know if his body would be returned to the ocean to provide nourishment to the marine ecosystem as a form of ecological restoration action. People also used words and emojis to express sorrow, heartbreak and love, which can be a form of emotion-focused coping. Meaning-focused coping may take the form of developing mourning practices. For Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw, mourning Notcho meant bringing him to their territory so “(we) could care for his remains in accordance with our laws,” and honouring him with a sacred ceremony . Many online responses expressed gratitude for the ceremony. Making meaning through mourning The need for specific mourning practices, like ceremonies or rituals, to mourn ecological losses was identified more than 30 years ago by Phyllis Windle, an ecologist and hospital chaplain. When it comes to ecological grief, some people may lack spiritual traditions to support them. Meaningful rituals can be difficult to create in a secularized society, and without precedent or cultural guidance, people may not know how to make meaning from these losses. Facebook users responding to the honouring ceremony of Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw demonstrated their desire for meaning-making through mourning practices in a variety of ways, from thanking everyone caring for Notcho’s journey, to expressing gratitude for learning about the honouring ceremony, to creating their own mourning practices. While some people find Indigenous beliefs and ceremonial practices inspiring , non-Indigenous people need to create practices rooted in their own beliefs and values . As a non-Indigenous person from Ontario, I do not claim any connection to Notcho or the waters he lived in, apart from a brief, magical encounter with a pod of breaching humpbacks in northern British Columbia a decade ago. Nonetheless, I cried when I heard how Notcho died and as I read people’s responses. I wondered whether the ferry passengers who witnessed his fatal injury experienced a form of secondary trauma and how they will cope. I also think about the conservation organizations and volunteers who love these whales and give their time to advocate for them. Do they have the practices and supports they need to mourn when they lose a whale they know? As an outsider, it may not be my place to create my own ritual for Notcho. What I have found is that telling a part of his story, with gratitude to those who knew him, has become my small way of making meaning from his death. Perhaps that is where many of us can begin when we experience ecological grief: we can let ourselves feel both love and sorrow for whales and other non-human parts of nature. And we can respectfully create ways of marking these losses that reflect our own values. Ecological grief is a sign of how much we care . Corina Brdar does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Mourning Notcho: What one whale’s death teaches us about ecological grief

articles.content: Delegates from around the world are currently gathering in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31 . Among the issues up for discussion will be an important question: who should pay for the harms caused by climate change? One study estimated that between 1850 and 2015, the Global North was responsible for 92 per cent of the carbon dioxide emissions that exceeded countries’ fair shares of a safe global limit. The United Nations Fund for responding to Loss and Damage , established at the 2022 COP in Egypt, has received requests from 119 countries seeking US$2.8 billion in funding , far more than the US$342 million allocated to its start-up phase. Canada committed CA$16 million , while the United States, the largest historical emitter, pledged US$17.5 million, then withdrew from the fund’s board in 2025. Decisions on the first regular round of funding requests are expected in December 2026 , but Nigeria’s environment minister expressed the frustration of many when he said in June that the fund “ looks like a mirage .” Behind the struggle over loss and damage is a question that extends beyond climate finance. What responsibilities do institutions that benefited from carbon-intensive development bear toward those living with the consequences, especially when some losses cannot be undone? Universities have their own climate debt to confront. “Climate change and planetary destruction have been accelerated, in large part, by technologies developed in universities,” as one of us, Mateus Tremembé, has written . Universities and climate change Universities have helped build and sustain the carbon-intensive economy in several ways. They have produced much of the knowledge it runs on, from petroleum engineering to economic models that treat continuous growth as a measure of progress . They have trained professionals who design, manage and finance that economy, often reinforcing the idea that land and nature are resources to be extracted. And many have maintained financial ties with fossil-fuel companies through research partnerships, donations and investments. Research can also reproduce extractive relationships, even in projects meant to help communities adapt to climate change. Local and Indigenous communities often contribute significant knowledge, labour and data , while academic researchers frequently retain control over the questions, funding, data and interpretation, and recognition flows disproportionately to universities. This imbalance runs counter to the CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance and article 31 of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples , which affirm Indigenous Peoples’ authority over their knowledge and data. Addressing these patterns requires a reparative approach to climate research: one built on long-term accountability to communities and their lands, redistributing resources and authority, and treating Indigenous and local knowledge as expertise rather than raw material. Research cannot undo irreversible losses. But where communities invite collaboration, it can support their efforts to respond to ecological change on their own terms. Importance of shared authority The distinction between providing resources and sharing authority is also central to debates over climate finance. The loss and damage fund describes its approach as “bottom-up, country-led and country-owned” , with provisions for local engagement. This is meant to counter the longstanding tendency for climate finance priorities to be set by international institutions and donors. But country ownership is not the same as community control . In many countries, governments have long made decisions about Indigenous lands and lives without Indigenous consent. Requiring national government endorsement does not guarantee that Indigenous Peoples will decide how losses in their territories are defined or addressed. This matters especially because many climate losses cannot be fully measured in money . They may involve broken relationships with rivers, plants and animals, cultural practices tied to place, or knowledge passed between generations. When governments and funders define losses only in monetary terms, these dimensions can disappear from view , along with communities’ own priorities for responding to them. Community-directed research Adaptation seeks to reduce climate risks. Loss and damage concerns harms that cannot be fully prevented or reversed. Both raise questions about who defines harm, what should be sustained or repaired and who directs the response. These questions inform our work on community-directed adaptation research , or C-DAR. The premise is simple but demanding: communities should lead in setting research questions and making decisions, with as much control over resources as possible. In Ceará, northeastern Brazil, the Tremembé da Barra do Mundaú Indigenous people are facing environmental pressures that affect their way of life, with climate change expected to bring more severe droughts and extreme rainfall . The community is developing collaborative research initiatives to strengthen traditional food systems , including collective farming, environmental education for young people and phasing out the use of pesticides. The Tremembé people have also drawn up their Territorial and Environmental Management Plan , a document that sets out community priorities for the management of natural resources and for maintaining traditional knowledge and practices. More than just a planning document, it represents a collective commitment to present and future generations: that children born in the territory will have access to drinking water, clean rivers, healthy fish, living forests and ancestral knowledge that is practised and passed on. For the Tremembé, protecting biodiversity also means ensuring the continuity of life, culture and relationships with their land. Repair involves sustaining the knowledge, practices and territorial conditions that communities identify as necessary for their collective futures. Following communities’ lead Under a community-directed adaptation approach, communities decide what data are collected, how they are used and who controls them. Academic research partners can support these efforts by following the community’s lead and contributing their skills when invited. In Tremembé territories, academic partners have supported the installation of weather stations to record rainfall and temperature, and young people are involved in assessing water security. The aim is to bring these data into conversation with Elders’ knowledge of how springs and rivers have changed and to inform climate adaptation planning. Ultimately, the value of such research should not be measured only by whether it contributes to academic knowledge, but by whether it strengthens a community’s ability to monitor ecological change, make adaptation decisions and sustain knowledge and relationships across generations. Communities are already responding to climate change, drawing on generational knowledge and relationships with their territories. Universities can contribute expertise, resources and infrastructure, but doing so requires following communities’ priorities and rethinking established research practices. As climate finance begins to tackle loss and damage, universities should begin confronting their own climate debt by shifting control over research priorities and resources toward communities. Sharon Stein receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada. articles.content: In July 2022, the late Pope Francis came to Canada seeking forgiveness for the Catholic Church’s role in the residential school system, acknowledging it as genocide . His penitential pilgrimage was intended to mark a new chapter in the relationship between the Catholic Church and Indigenous Peoples, calling for a renewed commitment of “ walking together .” Four years later, students at a Catholic high school in Grande Prairie, Alberta, offered a glimpse of what this commitment might look like in practice. On Oct. 13 , Indigenous and non-Indigenous students staged a demonstration to protest residential school denialism publicly endorsed by one of their social studies teachers on her personal Facebook page . They did so by walking out together. Their peaceful disobedience was more than an act of protest. It was an expression of solidarity, a collective refusal to dismiss Indigenous experiences and a reminder that reconciliation is advanced not only through institutional apologies, but through the actions of those willing to stand together against injustice. Challenge from inside Catholic institutions We are married writing partners and PhD students whose respective areas of study involve Catholic theology and religion curriculum in Catholic schools. We approach this research from Anishinaabe (Noah) and settler (Erenna) perspectives. We have previously examined how colonial ideologies of institutional leadership within Catholic education can undermine commitments to reconciliation . However, the Grande Prairie walkout offers an opportunity to consider the other side of this relationship: Students exercising their own agency at the grassroots level to challenge injustice from within a Catholic institution. Students were responding to a Facebook post by a social studies teacher at their high school on Sept. 30, the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, also known as Orange Shirt Day . The post shared a statement from Maxime Bernier, the leader of the People’s Party of Canada, which partly reads: “ Let’s tell the truth: no bodies were found in Kamloops. The residential-school ‘genocide’ claim is a hoax .” The teacher added “Hear, hear!” on her status update. Read more: We fact-checked residential school denialists and debunked their ‘mass grave hoax’ theory In an interview, the teacher told CBC News she is “not a residential school denialist, which many people have framed me as.” Reconciliation, resistance and solidarity For reconciliation to be meaningful, it must amount to more than institutional apologies and commemorations, especially when members of those institutions undermine the commitments made. In Red Skin, White Masks , Dene political scientist Glen Sean Coulthard argues that reconciliation focused on institutional forgiveness, without radically transforming colonial relationships, leaves Indigenous people vulnerable to ongoing harms. This is similarly the case when institutions fail to adequately prevent denialism. Read more: 5 ways teachers can respond to residential school denialism in the classroom Combating these institutional shortcomings often requires resistance. Coulthard says resistance is not an obstacle to reconciliation but an expression of Indigenous agency and self-determination. Seen this way, the Grande Prairie walkout was more than a protest against one teacher’s posts: It was students refusing to let reconciliation remain an institutional promise. Equally significant was the solidarity of the students who walked out together. Coulthard and Leanne Betasamosake Simpson, a Michi Saagiig Nishnaabeg scholar, describe solidarity rooted in mutual responsibility and collective resistance, not sympathy alone, in their article Grounded Normativity / Place-Based Solidarity . Such solidarity asks more of institutions that apologize while their own members or representatives deny the truth. It’s worth noting that the student walkout happened at a school named for Pope John Paul II, who in a 1979 address to young people stated: “ Liberation, even in the social sense, begins with knowledge and courageous proclamation of the truth .” Teaching for justice In a recent Warrior Life podcast interview, Mi'kmaw lawyer and author Pam Palmater spoke with Indigenous studies professor and writer Niigaan Sinclair and historian Sean Carleton about their newly published book, Truth Before Reconciliation: Confronting Residential School Denialism . Sinclair, a member of Peguis First Nation, notes that for over a century, Canadians have been miseducated and misinformed about the residential school system — yet younger generations are generally now being exposed to either courses or credentialed research on the topic of truth and reconciliation . This learning, we argue, instils a strong sense of historical and information literacy. All generations need opportunities to learn the same, and to identify and counter residential schools denialism. Read more: Confronting residential schools denialism is an ethical and shared Canadian responsibility A desire to counter denialism was exemplified by the young adults who stood up for the injustice and false narrative they observed by a member of their school community. One student stated at the walkout: “ My grandma was in residential schools, and I just don’t think this is OK. And I’m Kaska Dena too .” Another added: “ Young people should not be underestimated .” Indigenous and non-Indigenous student allies came together to exemplify unity in a matter that challenged their comfort and privilege. It requires the courage to confront misinformation, acknowledge historical realities and not only recognize truth, but defend it. Following the walkout, the Grande Prairie Catholic School Division issued a media release stating that: “ Our Catholic faith calls us to uphold the dignity of every person, listen with compassion and work toward justice and reconciliation .” The division pledged to advance truth and reconciliation through education, meaningful relationships and action. The students of St. John Paul II Catholic School remind us that the success of Catholic education should not be measured solely by what students learn about faith and justice , but by their willingness to act when faced with injustice. Perhaps the most hopeful sign of reconciliation is not simply that the next generation is learning to walk together, but that they are willing to walk out together. articles.description: In July 2022, the late Pope Francis came to Canada seeking forgiveness for the Catholic Church’s role in the residential school system, acknowledging it as genocide . His penitential pilgrimage was intended to mark a new chapter in the relationship between the Catholic Church and Indigenous Peoples, calling for a renewed commitment of “ walking together .” Four years later, students at a Catholic high school in Grande Prairie, Alberta, offered a glimpse of what this commitment might look like in practice. On Oct. 13 , Indigenous and non-Indigenous students staged a demonstration to protest residential school denialism publicly endorsed by one of their social studies teachers on her personal Facebook page . They did so by walking out together. Their peaceful disobedience was more than an act of protest. It was an expression of solidarity, a collective refusal to dismiss Indigenous experiences and a reminder that reconciliation is advanced not only through institutional apologies, but through the actions of those willing to stand together against injustice. Challenge from inside Catholic institutions We are married writing partners and PhD students whose respective areas of study involve Catholic theology and religion curriculum in Catholic schools. We approach this research from Anishinaabe (Noah) and settler (Erenna) perspectives. We have previously examined how colonial ideologies of institutional leadership within Catholic education can undermine commitments to reconciliation . However, the Grande Prairie walkout offers an opportunity to consider the other side of this relationship: Students exercising their own agency at the grassroots level to challenge injustice from within a Catholic institution. Students were responding to a Facebook post by a social studies teacher at their high school on Sept. 30, the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, also known as Orange Shirt Day . The post shared a statement from Maxime Bernier, the leader of the People’s Party of Canada, which partly reads: “ Let’s tell the truth: no bodies were found in Kamloops. The residential-school ‘genocide’ claim is a hoax .” The teacher added “Hear, hear!” on her status update. In Red Skin, White Masks , Dene political scientist Glen Sean Coulthard argues that reconciliation focused on institutional forgiveness, without radically transforming colonial relationships, leaves Indigenous people vulnerable to ongoing harms. This is similarly the case when institutions fail to adequately prevent denialism. articles.content: Facing tariffs and a deteriorating trade relationship, Canada has been looking to reduce its dependence on the United States, which still accounts for over 70 per cent of Canadian goods exports . Prime Minister Mark Carney has set a target of doubling exports to countries other than the U.S. over the next decade . China, which is already Canada’s second-largest trading partner, with about $125 billion of two-way merchandise trade in 2025 , is an obvious part of that strategy. But expanding trade with China brings its own risks. Its economy is facing mounting pressures , including a prolonged property-market downturn, a shrinking population and escalating trade tensions with the U.S. For Canada, the question is how resilient that relationship would be if the Chinese economy entered a prolonged slowdown. Could efforts to reduce dependence on one major trading partner leave Canada increasingly reliant on another? Japan’s experience offers a cautionary lesson. As Canada pursues trade diversification, it must be careful not to replace its dependence on the U.S. with a new dependence on China. The warning signs Japan’s economic trajectory offers a striking example of how quickly expectations of continued growth can unravel. In the 1980s, it was widely expected to challenge the U.S. for global economic dominance . Instead, the collapse of its property and stock market bubbles in the early 1990s ushered in decades of stagnation. Land prices fell for 14 straight years , with commercial land dropping to about one-third of the 1991 level . This period became known as Japan’s “lost decades.” China, now the world’s second-largest economy, faces some comparable pressures. Its property market has been in decline since 2021, eroding household wealth and weakening local government finances . Its population has fallen for four straight years , and the government’s 2026 growth target of 4.5 to five per cent is its lowest since 1991 . China is also facing escalating trade tensions with Washington. Restrictions on Chinese exports and access to advanced technologies have intensified the economic rivalry between the two countries. There are, however, important limits to the comparison. China’s economic structure, political system and global position are different from Japan’s. But Japan’s experience shows why Canada should weigh the risks before becoming overly reliant on another major trading partner. Why China is different Several key differences could send China down another path. Unlike Japan, it has a state-controlled banking system , which gives Beijing greater capacity to absorb losses or delay needed restructuring. China is also poorer and less urbanized than Japan was in 1990, leaving more room for growth in household wealth and domestic consumption. It has so far established leading positions in electric vehicles , batteries and solar panels . Its relationship with Washington is fundamentally different, too. Japan was a U.S. ally, and its trade disputes took place within an established security relationship. China, on the other hand, is a strategic rival that competes with the U.S. for influence. China has a population of 1.4 billion people but this doesn’t automatically translate into strong consumer demand. Household consumption is about 40 per cent of GDP, compared with an OECD average of about 60 per cent . That imbalance has contributed to China’s reliance on exports to sustain its growth. In 2025, net exports accounted for about one-third of its growth, the highest share since 1997 . What a slowdown means for Canada Canadian exports to China are heavily concentrated in commodities, which leaves them particularly exposed to changes in Chinese industrial activity and resource demand. Canadian energy exports rose about 78 per cent in 2025, reaching roughly $9.5 billion as the expansion of the Trans Mountain pipeline opened up greater access to overseas markets. But China’s oil demand is weakening , with further declines expected. A prolonged slowdown could accelerate that trend, reducing demand for Canadian energy and putting downward pressure on global commodity prices. Other Canadian exports are exposed to China’s property downturn. Steelmaking coal, copper and lumber, are the most tied to construction and infrastructure investment, so a prolonged contraction in the property sector would weaken demand for these materials. The geographic concentration of Canadian exports adds to the risk. Alberta and British Columbia accounted for 92 per cent of the recent growth in exports to China . Both provinces have substantial resource sectors and are particularly exposed to changes in Chinese commodity demand. Interdependence is not the same as trust Economic ties cannot be separated from political and security relationships. When trade is concentrated, governments can use access to supplies or export markets as leverage in disputes. During the trade disputes of the 1980s, Washington pressured Tokyo to open its markets. Japanese carmakers such as Honda and Toyota built plants across North America, including in Ontario , creating jobs and embedding Japanese investment in North America. The pattern continued under U.S. President Donald Trump. In 2025, Japan pledged US$550 billion in American investment as part of an agreement to resolve tariff disputes. In both cases, a longstanding political and security alliance provided a foundation for negotiating trade disagreements. Japan’s relationship with China offers a different lesson. During a territorial dispute in 2010, Japanese businesses reported Chinese shipments of rare earth minerals had stopped . This incident exposed Japan’s dependence on China for materials, and Japan subsequently worked to diversify its supply, cutting China’s share of its rare earth imports from about 90 per cent to 60-70 per cent . Canada has encountered a similar vulnerability. After imposing 100 per cent tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in 2024 , China responded with tariffs on canola. Exports to China subsequently fell 62 per cent . A deal reached in January lowered canola tariffs in exchange for allowing 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles into Canada annually at a 6.1 per cent tariff. Lessons for Canada Japan’s experience highlights two lessons in Canada’s push to diversify trade. The first is that an economic slowdown does not necessarily make a country an insignificant trading partner. Japan remained a wealthy and important market long after its property bubble burst. China, however, could face prolonged stagnation before reaching Japan’s level of affluence. If Chinese demand weakens, commodities producers will have to compete for a smaller pool of buyers. The second lesson is that the political relationship behind trade can matter as much as trade volume. Japan’s ties with the U.S. survived disputes partly because they ran both ways: Japanese firms built plants in North America, and the two countries shared security interests. Japan’s dependence on China demonstrated the risks of relying too heavily on a single source of important resources. Canada’s relationship with China is more asymmetric. Much of the trade involves Canadian commodities flowing one way, with market access Beijing can grant or withdraw. Trading dependence on Washington for dependence on Beijing would simply replace one vulnerability with another. Canada’s priority should be to expand its customer base. Its Pacific coast can ship crude, gas and critical minerals to Asia, while the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership gives Canada preferential access to Japan and other Indo-Pacific markets. Trading with more countries is not the same as having more freedom to choose. The goal is to ensure that no single partner — whether rival or ally — can set the terms. Amir Bahman Radnejad is affiliated with Canadian Global Affair Institute. Masaru Karube is affiliated with the Institute of Innovation Research, Hitotsubashi University, Japan.

articles.content: Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced a plan in the 2026 federal budget aimed at eliminating homelessness in the next decade. A statement about the plan says homelessness “strikes at the heart of Canadian values of fairness, solidarity, and human dignity.” What are these values and how exactly are they impacted by homelessness? The announcement does not clearly answer these questions. As a researcher in public health ethics, I want to fill the gaps by drawing on empirical and philosophical research to explain why, exactly, the urgent need to address homelessness is matter of ethics. Eroding dignity Dignity refers to a kind of inherent worth that all people hold equally by virtue of being human. It serves as the foundation for human rights, which provide people with entitlements and establish obligations for others (including governments) to treat people in ways that respect their rights. Violations of those human rights , which include a guarantee to adequate housing , are one way people experience a loss of dignity when homeless. Some policy responses to homeless encampments have also violated rights guaranteed under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and therefore peoples’ dignity . Homelessness violates dignity in other ways. A lack of shelter, housing and a home — understood as a place of belonging — leads people to experience shame and ostracism. Homelessness excludes people from meaningful participation in social life. That leaves them on the margins of society, with little to no resources or options, reduced social status and a lack of freedom and authority over their lives since much of what they do, even just to survive, is criminalized . In these ways, homelessness reduces people to being less-than, unworthy, and unequal. What makes a just society? This brings us to fairness and related questions about what a just society looks like. In one view , a just society involves how people stand in terms of equality with one another rather than in hierarchic relations. The failure of the state to adequately respond to homelessness is a profound injustice because it demonstrates a lack of equal concern for some of the most vulnerable members of society. And, as some argue , this is precisely what’s at play in terms of homelessness. Another famous view comes from American philosopher John Rawls . For him, justice as fairness is concerned with the distribution of benefits and burdens in society, according to two principles . The first principle states that everyone has an equal claim to basic liberties. The relevant part of the second principle, called the difference principle, holds that any social and economic inequalities in a just society should give the greatest benefit to the least advantaged members of society. Although this view tolerates some inequality, homelessness remains incompatible with its principles of justice. Rawls didn’t name housing as one of the benefits to be distributed under these principles. Some scholars have argued that it must be one of the social goods we should be concerned about distributing fairly, through, say, social housing models. The fact that homelessness exists to the degree it does in a wealthy country like Canada does in fact suggest a lack of fairness in a broader distributive sense. Some people are left without shelter altogether, some have subpar shelter while others have plenty. But the causes of homelessness are complex and multi-faceted . The problem has been made worse by a lack of affordable housing, higher unemployment and overall higher costs of living associated with rising inflation. In research on the causes, experts and advocates agree that it’s not caused by the choices people make, but the choices we make as a society . Health inequities Such social choices have ripple effects, as people who experience homelessness face risks to their health and well-being. Homelessness disproportionately affects some populations , which can lead to vicious cycles of poor health, higher risk of infectious disease and premature death . Homelessness therefore leads to inequities in health. Homelessness is an affront to human dignity, and it’s unfair. The concept of solidarity speaks to the need for society generally to address injustices as a collective. Failing to do so results in the social and moral abandonment of people experiencing homelessness as they are left to suffer the injustices of homelessness alone. While these arguments make a compelling ethical case for ending homelessness, the real work lies in translating justification into action. In addition to monitoring and evaluating the practical outcomes of the promised federal funds, Canadians should not lose sight of the ethical values underpinning them and the overarching goal of ending homelessness. We need to ensure our policies not only reflect our ethical values, but also produce outcomes that actively support them. We must consider whether the policies and programs implemented align with our ethical values, and whether their outcomes are effective in promoting them as well. Nicole Fice has received funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council for a project on the ethics of encampment evictions.

articles.content: Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia — an American tech giant that designs and manufactures graphics processing units — has resigned following a controversy that exposed an uncomfortable question for western democracies: Can they pursue economic engagement with China while protecting the companies and technologies central to national security? Canada’s renewed commercial ties with Beijing make the question a pressing one. What’s alleged The New York Times has reported that United States intelligence officials suspected Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, of passing information to Chinese intelligence. Megaspeed is an an artificial intelligence cloud infrastructure and data centre provider The newspaper added that officials had discovered a close relationship between her and Jensen Huang, who is not related to her. On Nov. 8, Nvidia announced an independent investigation while stating that it had no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. Before his resignation, Jensen Huang acknowledged in a message to staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife . Three U.S. House committee chairs have requested a closed-door briefing with him, while China rejects the spying allegations . The reach of foreign interference No public finding establishes that Jensen Huang knowingly assisted foreign intelligence or that restricted information was compromised. Whether Megaspeed’s chips reached Chinese users through data centres in Malaysia and Indonesia is also being investigated. Suspected technology diversion and a suspected intelligence operation are different claims, and each requires its own evidence. Singapore says its investigating Megaspeed but has not investigated Alice Huang . The Nvidia case shows that foreign interference reaches well beyond election meddling. When the target is a leading AI-chip supplier globally, the stakes extend to export controls and threatens national security. Canada’s Hogue Commission focused on interference in democratic institutions, while the 2025 CSIS public report goes further, identifying businesses, universities and researchers as targets of espionage and covert influence. Read more: New commission sheds light on how diaspora communities are impacted by foreign interference Foreign interference beyond elections Commercial relationships and personal networks can provide access to sensitive information and influential decision-makers. Gray-zone scholarship explains how states may pursue advantages through gradual, deniable actions that fall short of open conflict. Studies of Chinese influence operations describe the long-term cultivation of influential people and organizations. The concern arises when relationships, economic leverage and information operations combine in a co-ordinated effort to manipulate decisions. Personal relationships can also become instruments of influence. Oliver August’s 2007 book, Inside the Red Mansion: On the Trail of China’s Most Wanted Man , traced the rise of Xiamen businessman Lai Changxing. His lavish entertainment complex, the Red Mansion , reportedly provided officials with women and other favours. Lai fled to Canada in 1999 and fought removal for about 12 years; eventually, he was deported in July 2011 . In 2012, a Xiamen court sentenced him to life in prison for smuggling and bribery. Lai’s case involved corruption, not espionage. Still, if the Nvidia allegations are proven, they would point to a familiar technique — the “honey trap” — used in influence operations to leverage personal relationships for access to powerful people. Canada has experienced economic coercion first-hand. After the 2018 arrest of Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou, China restricted imports of Canadian farm products and detained Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor. The Meng Wanzhou dispute showed how commercial and diplomatic ties can become levers of pressure. Read more: Meng and the two Michaels: Why China’s hostage diplomacy failed Trade diversification vs. strategic rivalry Canada’s renewed engagement with China is understandable. American tariffs and President Donald Trump’s “51st state” remarks have unsettled Canada’s closest economic relationship. In January 2026, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a new strategic partnership with China. Canada introduced an annual quota of 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles at a 6.1 per cent tariff . Amid Oshawa auto layoffs , the move sparked debate about industrial policy, though the layoffs cannot simply be blamed on Chinese imports. Canadian and Chinese defence officials also resumed military dialogue after eight years . Canadian cabinet ministers recently met Vice Premier He Lifeng to expand economic co-operation. Canada aims to raise exports to China by 50 per cent by 2030. Wider market access may reduce dependence on the U.S., but it can also create vulnerabilities if security safeguards lag. Structural realism , associated with U.S. political scientist Kenneth Waltz, explains such tension: without a central authority to guarantee their security, states keep competing over sensitive technology. American AI-chip export restrictions are one expression of that rivalry. The Arctic raises the stakes Canada has announced more than $35 billion in federal northern and Arctic investments and a defence industrial strategy emphasizing dual-use technology, domestic innovation and secure supply chains. China’s dominance of rare-earth processing creates another dependency. The International Energy Agency estimates China supplied 91 per cent of refined magnet rare earths in 2024. Some export controls are active although others have been suspended. Canadian Arctic security assessments also identify Chinese interest in research, infrastructure and critical minerals. The risks go beyond mining. Arctic communications, remote sensing, drones and data infrastructure can serve civilian and defence purposes simutaneously. That makes partnerships valuable but sensitive. As with Nvidia, the core question is who gains access to technology, operational data and intellectual property — and on what terms. Read more: Chinese scientists are increasingly shaping the future of the Arctic amid China’s rising presence Engage, but protect Canada needs a practical security agenda. Governments should brief executives and researchers on recruitment and information risks. Firms should strengthen safeguards around intellectual property and supply chains and give employees confidential ways to disclose conflicts of interest and report suspected coercion. Intelligence agencies and industry associations should establish trusted channels for reporting suspicious approaches. Regulators should apply existing national-security investment screening and co-ordinate oversight of dual-use technologies, while protecting legitimate academic exchange and Indigenous authority over northern projects. None of this means treating Chinese Canadians, Chinese firms, ordinary trade or employees’ private lives as suspect. It means separating lawful engagement from covert coercion, based on evidence. The Nvidia investigation is unfinished and espionage has not been proved. The immediate lesson is that commercial openness needs credible safeguards. Canada can diversify its trade without trading away its capacity to make independent security decisions. articles.content: Physical education should encourage healthy relationships with movement and exercise. (Salah Regouane/Unsplash) In June 2026, the Alberta government released an updated draft of its Grades 7 to 9 Physical Education and Wellness curriculum , intended for optional classroom piloting during the 2026–27 school year and mandatory implementation in September 2027. The way food, bodies and physical activity are discussed in the new curriculum has the potential to prime, endorse or worsen disordered eating and compulsive exercise among youth. Adolescence is a time when youth become more preoccupied with their appearance and experience greater body dissatisfaction . They are also at a higher risk for developing disordered eating behaviours , including dieting, food restriction and binge eating, which can precede eating disorders. Because patterns of dieting and disordered eating in teenage years can persist into adulthood , it’s vital to help young people develop healthy relationships with their bodies. Our research on the conditions that foster eating disorders and body dissatisfaction compels us to speak out and identify the key issues with the proposed curriculum. Health cannot be reduced to weight Throughout the curriculum, higher body weight is framed in relatively simplistic terms, with an emphasis on overeating. For example, one learning outcome states: “Larger portions can lead to overconsumption and increase risk of obesity and chronic disease.” Obesity is a complex, chronic disease with several contributing factors outside of direct control, including genetics, access to physical recreation opportunities and safe neighbourhoods, socioeconomic class and medication side effects. Teaching students that obesity is simply the result of overconsumption risks blaming individuals for their body weight and creating the misleading impression that body size and shape are entirely within their control. Students in larger bodies, or who have family members in larger bodies, are likely to feel blamed and shamed in these lessons. Such simplistic messages can also reinforce weight-based bullying , which is already too common in Canadian schools and has worrying consequences for the health of both victims and bystanders , including an increased risk of eating disorders . Instead of focusing on weight, health education should emphasize behaviours that benefit all dimensions of well-being, regardless of body size. Food is not inherently good or bad The draft curriculum creates a binary distinction between good and bad foods by casting convenient and ultra-processed foods in a negative light. Yet these are inconsistently defined concepts . For example, a Grade 7 learning outcome states: “Modern diets that include ultra-processed foods and convenience foods can be high in calories (energy) and low in nutrients.” Similarly, an outcome in Grade 8 reads: “Compared with processed foods, whole foods harvested from the land absorb nutrients from the soil, enhancing their taste, quality, appearance and nutritional value.” Food binaries attach moral value to food, potentially shaming students who do not have access to the “right” foods. A restrictive, fear-based approach to food can result in out-of-control eating or rigid food avoidance , both of which are forms of disordered eating. These concerns are particularly relevant in Alberta, which is currently experiencing one of the highest rates of food insecurity in the country . Many families rely on food banks, which often distribute processed or convenience foods. Students should not feel ashamed of eating what their families can afford or access, particularly when food insecurity itself can heighten the risk of eating disorders . Instead, students should be taught to approach food intuitively and flexibly based on their access and needs to fuel daily living activities. Tracking food and exercise can backfire Perhaps the most concerning curriculum outcomes are those that ask students to monitor their dietary and exercise patterns and develop personal plans to achieve nutrition and fitness goals and framing “wellness apps” as a helpful resource to do so. Such assignments risk reinforcing the idea that eating and activity patterns are solely within a person’s control. They overlook whether youth have a choice in what food is available in their homes or the privilege of accessing physical activity in safe environments. Evaluating teenagers on behaviours they have little to no control over can set them up for feeling like failures, ashamed or discouraged. Food and exercise tracking are also associated with eating disorders and should not be required school assignments. Despite the widespread promotion of food and exercise tracking tools and apps, research suggests they are relatively ineffective at improving eating and exercise habits and can increase body concerns, disordered eating and compulsive exercise. Wellness apps and tracking devices are not only more attractive to people who have pre-existing eating and body concerns , but can also initiate these preoccupations and disordered behaviours and therefore should not be encouraged in schools. Physical activity is more than appearance The new curriculum risks presenting physical fitness and athletic performance as central reasons for engaging in physical activity. It emphasizes concepts that are specific to muscle building at competitive levels, such as overload, specificity, reversibility and the principle of diminishing returns. Media portrayals of these practices and ideals of muscularity are associated with increased body dissatisfaction and muscle dysmorphia in Canadian youth . Emphasizing these concepts in general health education risks reinforcing a narrow understanding of physical activity centred on physical performance and a preoccupation with muscularity . The language around “personal fitness” could also encourage the idealization of thinness and muscularity as the standard and metric of “health,” rather than teaching students how enjoying movement can create benefits for our bodies, minds, relationships and emotions throughout their lifespan. A broader perspective is needed Physical and health education can play an important role in helping students develop a healthy relationship with food and movement. These topics should not be avoided. Rather, schools need evidence-based health education that is developmentally appropriate, eating disorder-safe, weight neutral , inclusive of those experiencing food insecurity and situated within a broader understanding of adolescent health. For ideas on keeping class discussions weight-neutral and assignments safe and developmentally appropriate, visit the Body Image Research Lab at the University of Calgary, where we research body image, eating disorders and weight bias. Shelly Russell-Mayhew receives funding from Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council. articles.content: Protests took place in cities across Canada today against a proposed bill that some fear could undermine environmental protections as well as the rights of workers and Indigenous communities. The Canadian government introduced Bill C-39 , the Building Canada Strong Act, in September 2026, with the stated aim of fast-tracking large-scale projects. Hailed as a major advancement by the government, it has also been criticized as a bill that could bulldoze environmental regulations . The government has said the proposed legislation is aimed at protecting “economic security.” Under the new bill, new “federal economic zones” would be created where projects could be “pre-approved.” This would provide exceptions to habitat and species-at-risk protections and other federal oversight. What could this new legislation mean for environmental regulations and how could it impact Canadians if passed into law? Less time for environmental review In October 2024, the government released a framework for implementing the right to a healthy environment under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, linking environmental protection directly to human health and well-being . However, Bill C-39 reduces the time period for thorough environmental review. The government has touted the bill’s shortened timeline for project approval, compressed to a one-year review . This allows for quick decisions to be made, and proponents to know whether a specific project will be able to proceed in a shorter timeframe. While this is viewed as a clear advantage, some are warning that the one-year timeline could still be extended and delayed . Environmental regulations are not simply environmental protections, they also protect public health. Effective regulations reduce exposure to polluted air, contaminated water, toxic chemicals and climate-related hazards. They help prevent disease, improve quality of life, reduce health-care costs and protect the well-being of current and future generations. Recent evidence shows that the health and economic benefits of environmental regulation far outweigh the relative costs. Build first, assess later Under Bill C-39, the government would be able to permit preliminary construction to begin before the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada completes an assessment. This would be the case if the environment minister considers a project to be in the “public interest.” Reduced environmental regulations would directly impact the communities within the area of the proposed projects and those downstream. It could mean potential environmental degradation and destruction, as well as weakened habitat protection, before a full assessment can be done . Many of the proposed “projects of public interest” are in areas of significant ecological importance. Many are situated on or near First Nations territories. Leaders from the Nishnawbe Aski Nation stated they “will not accept this legislation as it stands,” stating they support responsible development but that acceleration of development cannot be at the expense of Indigenous communities . The government is wrong in assuming the choice is either environmental protection or rapid development. Many jurisdictions have shown that projects can move faster when governments improve co-ordination across departments and agencies. This could include digitizing permitting, establishing clear timelines, conducting strategic planning earlier and eliminating duplication in approval processes. The evidence suggests that delays often arise from fragmented governance and administrative inefficiencies, not environmental safeguards. Pay now, worry later Bill C-39 also introduces changes to the Fisheries Act that make it easier to advance projects that may impact fish or fish habitats. The bill introduces third-party “habitat credits” and fees for minor impacts. Under this model, a third party can engage in habitat restoration and effectively “sell” credits to companies building major projects. The bill would allow companies that damage fish habitat during construction to buy habitat restoration credits from approved conservation groups instead of doing the restoration work themselves. The goal is to speed up project approvals while still requiring companies to compensate for environmental damage. Supporters say this could fund larger and more effective habitat restoration projects , reducing red tape without comprising environmental monitoring. Critics worry it could make it easier for companies to damage fish habitats as long as they can afford to pay for credits elsewhere, allowing habitat damage to become simply a cost of doing business. Media coverage of Bill C-39 tends to focus on pipelines, mines and regulatory processes. However, it’s also about the air Canadians breathe and the water they drink. It is about the fish we catch and the natural spaces that support our health and well-being. The question is not whether Canada should build new projects or strengthen its economy. It must. The real question is whether it can do so without weakening environmental safeguards that protect communities, ecosystems and future generations. As governments push to accelerate development, Canadians should pay close attention. The consequences will be felt not only in boardrooms and construction sites. They will be felt in rivers, forests and households across the country for decades to come. Kerry Black receives funding from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council Canada.

articles.content: For newcomers to Montréal’s Parc-Extension neighbourhood , the William-Hingston Centre was a place to find several kinds of supports under one roof. As the largest community centre in the area, it housed 15 community groups in a neighbourhood where roughly 14,000 people rely on local organizations each month . They included Afrique au Féminin , which offered women’s support; the Comité d'action de Parc-Extension , which provided housing assistance; and the Parc-Extension Youth Organization , which ran youth programming. That changed in 2021 , when the Centre de services scolaire de Montréal (CSSDM), which owns the building, notified the groups of plans for major renovations. All 15 groups were required to relocate by June 2025 at the latest. The timing could hardly have been worse: the neighbourhood was already grappling with land speculation and rising rents . The mass eviction has placed further pressure on a vulnerable immigrant community. But what happened at William-Hingston is not an isolated case. It’s part of a citywide pattern that reflects a growing tendency for the state to transfer responsibility for addressing social problems to private entities . Gentrification meets a loss of services Parc-Extension is one of Montréal’s most multicultural and economically vulnerable neighbourhoods. It’s home to a large number of families and immigrants: 69 per cent of residents speak a mother tongue other than French or English, and 39 per cent of the population living in low income, compared with 21 per cent for the city of Montréal as a whole. Over the past few years, the neighbourhood has faced rapid land speculation and rising evictions . The inauguration of the Université de Montréal’s Campus MIL, which straddles Parc-Extension’s southern border, has sparked waves of displacement, with rent increases disproportionately affecting the most vulnerable residents. Following their displacement, the William-Hingston groups had to seek new locations within Montréal’s competitive and increasingly unaffordable real estate market, while already operating with limited staffing and insufficient funding. Only seven managed to remain in the neighbourhood, divided between public-sector facilities, such as park chalets and arenas, and privately operated spaces that placed a significant financial burden on them. Five were forced to leave Parc-Extension altogether, distancing them from the people they served . People now have to travel to multiple locations to access the community support they need. At least one service disappeared entirely: the Parc-Extension Youth Organization lost its low-cost cafeteria following an eviction, serving its final meal in March 2024 after being part of the community for 22 years . The large turnout at that last meal underscored the community’s growing needs at a time when available services were declining. Community groups struggling to survive In Community-Based Action Research (CBAR) network meetings, organizers in Parc-Extension have expressed deep frustration with the current situation. Rose Ndjel, director of Afrique au Féminin , emphasized the importance of keeping community groups together in a central, shared location, such as the former William Hingston Centre . That kind of co-location was particularly vital for newly arrived immigrant families. In one building, they could find housing support, women’s programs, library services, French-language courses and food assistance. Losing that centralized access disrupts established networks of support and contributes to the broader fragmentation of a local care ecosystem that remains vital to residents. A citywide pattern of evictions The eviction of community groups from CSSDM-owned sites is becoming a recurring trend in Montréal. In communications between CSSDM and the city, the reason given has been the need for urgent major renovations . In Hochelaga-Maisonneuve, 11 community groups were evicted by the CSSDM , further undermining a neighbourhood already grappling with gentrification and evictions. In Ahuntsic, 13 community groups faced eviction last year by the CSSDM in 2024 . Even more concerning, in some cases, the CSSDM is selling surplus buildings to the private market and it’s already announced plans to sell some of its buildings in Rosemont, Ahuntsic, Saint-Michel and Plateau-Mont-Royal . No sale of William-Hingston has been announced, but the experience of other neighbourhoods seems to be a warning. Most of these changes have happened since 2020, when the Montréal school commissioners was abolished and replaced by the CSSDM. Since then, there has been no local political counterpart with whom to discuss the future of surplus school buildings accentuating the centralization of power to the provincial level . Previously, elected representatives offered a more accessible point of contact, and some were more willing to engage constructively with residents and community organizations. Today, decisions are made more directly by the ministry of education, and it has become much harder for neighbourhood concerns to be heard and addressed . Combined with a lack of investment in community organizations and buildings at both the municipal and provincial levels, these changes have left community groups uncertain about their future. Québec, as a province, is moving away from a model in which community groups are primarily supported by public funding and housed in government-owned buildings. Instead, they are increasingly expected to develop and finance new community centres themselves, without adequate public support and despite lacking the necessary resources and expertise all while having terrible working conditions. This has led to Le Communautaire à Boutte (the community sector is fed up), a provincial grassroots movement demanding more funding and recognition from the provincial government . In Parc-Extension, the Table de quartier de Parc-Extension , a local social development collaborative forum, is working to develop a new community centre on city-owned land with federal support . Provincial funding, however, is still pending. As the situation in Parc-Extension illustrates, this transfer of responsibility risks exacerbating vulnerabilities and contributing to this trend of eviction. This article was co-authored by Lucas Raimbault, a development agent at Bureau d'information de Parc-Extension. articles.description: For newcomers to Montréal’s Parc-Extension neighbourhood , the William-Hingston Centre was a place to find several kinds of supports under one roof. As the largest community centre in the area, it housed 15 community groups in a neighbourhood where roughly 14,000 people rely on local organizations each month . They included Afrique au Féminin , which offered women’s support; the Comité d'action de Parc-Extension , which provided housing assistance; and the Parc-Extension Youth Organization , which ran youth programming. That changed in 2021 , when the Centre de services scolaire de Montréal (CSSDM), which owns the building, notified the groups of plans for major renovations. All 15 groups were required to relocate by June 2025 at the latest. The timing could hardly have been worse: the neighbourhood was already grappling with land speculation and rising rents . The mass eviction has placed further pressure on a vulnerable immigrant community. But what happened at William-Hingston is not an isolated case. It’s part of a citywide pattern that reflects a growing tendency for the state to transfer responsibility for addressing social problems to private entities . Gentrification meets a loss of services Parc-Extension is one of Montréal’s most multicultural and economically vulnerable neighbourhoods. It’s home to a large number of families and immigrants: 69 per cent of residents speak a mother tongue other than French or English, and 39 per cent of the population living in low income, compared with 21 per cent for the city of Montréal as a whole. Over the past few years, the neighbourhood has faced rapid land speculation and rising evictions . The inauguration of the Université de Montréal’s Campus MIL, which straddles Parc-Extension’s southern border, has sparked waves of displacement, with rent increases disproportionately affecting the most vulnerable residents. Only seven managed to remain in the neighbourhood, divided between public-sector facilities, such as park chalets and arenas, and privately operated spaces that placed a significant financial burden on them. Five were forced to leave Parc-Extension altogether, distancing them from the people they served . People now have to travel to multiple locations to access the community support they need. articles.content: AI can improve our understanding of climate risks, but turning that knowledge into effective, equitable action will still depend on people and the decisions they are equipped to make. (Unsplash) Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has described COP31, being hosted in his country, as the “ implementation COP ,” emphasizing the need to translate climate commitments into action. The urgency is mounting. In September, the latest United Nations Environment Programme report concluded that limiting global warming to 1.5 C, or even slightly exceeding that threshold, is no longer achievable . Although returning below 1.5 C later this century remains possible, it would require rapid, substantial emissions reductions. Meanwhile, continued warming increases the risks of severe and irreversible climate impacts, making effective action critical. Given this urgency, artificial intelligence (AI) is attracting attention for its potential to deepen our understanding of climate risks and inform our responses. This growing interest is reflected in COP31’s Antalya AI Pledge . But realizing this potential raises an important question: Do the professionals working on climate adaptation have the knowledge, skills and support to use these technologies effectively and responsibly? AI and climate monitoring A 2023 national survey of Canadian professionals found that many do not feel adequately equipped to apply adaptation tools or make the case for adaptation measures. This points to a gap between understanding climate risks and having the capabilities to address them. Canada’s National Adaptation Strategy sets a target for 70 per cent of relevant professionals to have these capabilities by 2027. Canada uses AI to improve weather forecasting , and Canadian researchers use it to assess flood risks . Emerging applications include infrastructure and adaptation planning, such as flood-risk modelling in Vancouver . Yet better information does not necessarily lead to better decisions. As AI enters climate risk assessment and adaptation planning, it adds to the challenges professionals already face as they grapple with difficult decisions about infrastructure, public safety, ecosystems and community resilience. Read more: Adaptation policies must be built around the local communities facing climate change AI skills for a climate workforce The challenge goes beyond learning to use AI. Front-line climate action professionals need to understand how AI-generated information is produced, assess its reliability and limitations, and decide when and how to use it alongside other evidence and knowledge. Consider a coastal community facing rising flood risk. AI-supported modelling might identify vulnerable roads, homes and public facilities. But deciding whether to reinforce a shoreline, restore wetlands, restrict development or consider relocation involves more than comparing projected risks. These choices affect livelihoods, ecosystems and relationships to place. They also involve competing priorities and values, Indigenous rights and jurisdiction and questions about whose knowledge informs decisions and who has the authority to act. Many of the competencies required to navigate these challenges are already recognized in climate adaptation practice. At the ResilienceByDesign Lab at Royal Roads University, we’ve developed a Climate Action Competency Framework that identifies systems thinking, critical assessment of information, collaboration, communication and ethical leadership as essential to effective climate action. These capabilities remain relevant as AI enters adaptation practice, but they are insufficient on their own. Professionals also need to understand how AI systems work, recognize potential biases and gaps in the data they use, assess the reliability of AI-generated recommendations and navigate questions of transparency and accountability. This does not mean every planner, engineer, emergency manager or public health professional needs to become an AI specialist. Instead, they need enough AI literacy to ask informed questions, recognize when additional expertise is required and exercise professional judgment rather than simply accepting what the AI produces. From competence to professional practice Identifying these capabilities is only part of the challenge. They must also be reflected in professional standards, education, ongoing training and the organizational conditions that shape adaptation decisions. The Professions Advancing Adaptation Competencies initiative offers a Canadian example. By examining how the Climate Action Competency Framework aligns with the standards and practices of engineering, planning, accounting and landscape architecture, the initiative identified shared competencies and profession-specific needs. AI can improve our understanding of climate risks, but turning that knowledge into effective action depends on people and the decisions they are equipped to make. (Unsplash) Similar work could examine how AI is reshaping adaptation practice across professions, what existing competencies remain relevant and where additional capabilities are needed. This would strengthen workforce readiness by identifying the competencies professionals need to use emerging technologies effectively, rather than assuming that access to AI alone will automatically improve climate action. If COP31 is to deliver on its promise to move from commitments to implementation, preparing the workforce responsible for adaptation must be a priority. Governments, professional associations and educators must ensure professionals have the competencies, resources and institutional support to use these technologies responsibly and translate climate knowledge into action. AI can improve our understanding of climate risks, but turning that knowledge into effective, equitable action will still depend on people and the decisions they are equipped to make. Robin Cox has previously received research funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada and Natural Resources Canada.
