articles.content: What would it mean to teach students who are learning academic writing to use AI in “ethical” ways — for example, large language model (LLM) chatbots like ChatGPT, a specific form of GenAI? In rhetoric and writing studies, guiding documents on the teaching of writing and literature caution against all-out bans and call for guidance on ethically incorporating LLMs into writing. My institution, the University of Victoria, is “ committed to support the use of AI in transparent, responsible, ethical and equitable ways .” In the context of teaching writing, “ethics” and AI tends to be shorthand for academic integrity, informed by questions about composing and authorship , transparency and the writing process . However, even when ethical guidance around AI use includes reflecting on when AI is appropriate at all, this often assumes, as a foregone conclusion, that ethical AI use is a possibility. AI has environmental costs , and raises profound social and human concerns . We are doing students learning academic writing a disservice if we don’t think more broadly about what “ethical” use means. Classrooms are political spaces Writing is inherently bound up with power, and many writing studies scholars and teachers see classrooms as inherently political spaces. They focus on practices that equip students to add their voices to academic conversations, without compromising their ways of knowing. For these scholars, classrooms are places to develop anti-racist , equitable and inclusive practices. Many encourage students to question power and privilege , especially in first-year writing classrooms. Students learn to build arguments, organize evidence and communicate effectively to specific audiences. They gain transferable skills and experiences that can be foundational for structuring the rest of post-secondary life. Read more: How a first-year university writing course for Indigenous students fostered skills and belonging Tyler Branson , a professor of literature who also teaches composition, describes how “we might be better off thinking of first-year writing as a course in the practice of citizenship” instead of a course in academic writing. He argues that “society needs students skilled in civic discourse now more than ever.” A larger sphere of ethical inquiry We should provide students with reasons for and opportunities to resist and refuse GenAI. In reasoning about this, I draw on my training in rhetoric to ask what rhetorical scholar Judy Z. Segal calls “prior questions:” Asking “what” and “why” rather than starting from the basis of “how.” As Segal explains, rather than asking, for example: “How to make cosmetic surgery safer?” we might ask “How and why it is possible that we see ourselves in need of improvement via cosmetic surgery in the first place”? Educators should be asking “prior questions” around ethical use of LLM chatbots. When we think about these “how” questions in relation to LLM chatbots and the first-year writing classroom — “How to teach students to engage with these ethically and responsibly?” — we need to step back and consider what “ethical” means. ‘Writing involves making ethical choices’ In the collection Naming What We Know: Threshold Concepts of Writing Studies , John Duffy , professor of English at the University of Notre Dame, contributes a short essay, “Writing Involves Making Ethical Choices.” According to Duffy, every time we write for another person, we’re proposing a relationship with the reader or readers. He’s particularly interested in ethical questions for writers such as: “What kind of person do I want to be? How should I treat others? How should I live my life?” With the prevalence of GenAI, how we choose to write, and not just to whom and about what, has become a site of ethical choices as well. What values are normalized? When educators in writing classes make choices about how to engage with LLM chatbots or other forms of GenAI, we must expand our ideas of ethics beyond authorship and academic integrity. We should also discuss environmental impacts, exploitative offshore labour and how the logic of economic markets is affecting key resource use (energy, water, land and minerals) and arguments for (and against) adoption. As media studies expert Kate Crawford reminds us, theories of AI must account for “the states and corporations that drive and dominate it, the extractive industries that leave an imprint on the planet, the mass capture of data and the profoundly unequal and increasingly exploitative labour practices that sustain it.” If educators default to “how” to use AI ethically in our classrooms, we bypass a more fundamental question of: “What makes us think this is ethical in the first place?” Expectations, habits, norms Drawing on the logic of “prior concerns,” educators should reflect on what values we encourage or normalize when we tell students that it’s OK to turn to ChatGPT and how these values could shape expectations, habits and norms. Research has shown, for example, that ChatGPT uses lavish, qualitative praise as a default setting . Will this instant feedback realistically prepare students for participating in human networks, including receiving feedback from teachers or peers? If writing instructors normalize turning to an LLM chatbot for discussion, we also risk normalizing students’ avoidance of the effort it takes to talk to someone at the writing centre, visit office hours or consult a librarian. The ‘AI refusal’ approach in writing studies One solution is turning to the “GenAI refusal” approach in writing studies . Writing studies scholars Jennifer Sano-Franchini, Megan McIntyre and Maggie Fernandes position refusal as a “ disciplinary and principled response ” to GenAI use in the writing classroom. They offer 10 reasons that refusal is a warranted response to GenAI. While each of these reasons is persuasive, I point to number 10: “Refusal can be a principled and pragmatic response to the incursion of GenAI technologies in college writing courses. ” Writing instructors are in a position to help our students think critically about what responsibilities we have to each other, the world and its future. As inherently political spaces, first-year writing courses in particular should provide students with reasons to resist and refuse GenAI, and opportunities to do so. Loren Gaudet does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.content: Canada’s efforts to reduce international student numbers have had a striking effect in Atlantic Canada. Universities in the region have lost nearly half their international students in three years. According to preliminary figures released in October , international enrolment fell by 3,020 students (18 per cent) in the past year. That brings the decline since federal restrictions began in January 2024 to almost 48 per cent. Canada’s restrictions aim to address national concerns, but their effects vary across the country. The sharp decline in Atlantic Canada raises questions about whether federal policy takes enough account of smaller provinces. Read more: International students cap falsely blames them for Canada’s housing and health-care woes A decline beyond expectations In 2024, Ottawa introduced a cap on international student study permit applications. The government cited rapid growth, housing pressures and concerns about oversight. The government subsequently set further limits on international student enrolments for 2026. There were good reasons for reform. International student recruitment had grown quickly, and governments needed to ensure that institutions could support the students they admitted. Yet the scale and distribution of the decline have surprised even federal officials. In March, Canada’s Auditor General reported that the restrictions had reduced new study permit approvals more sharply than expected. Ottawa anticipated declines of no more than 10 per cent in several smaller provinces, including all four Atlantic provinces. It even expected an increase in Newfoundland and Labrador. Instead, approvals fell by at least 59 per cent in these provinces. The federal immigration department could not explain why approval rates fell so far below expectations. Allocating study permit applications to provinces does not guarantee that students will receive permits, accept university offers or enrol. Nor can the entire enrolment decline be blamed on the federal cap. Student applications, permit approval rates, financial pressures and Canada’s appeal as a study destination also affect enrolment. The scene at Memorial University Where I work in the faculty of education at Memorial University in Newfoundland, international enrolment fell from 4,889 students in 2023 to 2,682 in fall 2026 , a decrease of more than 45 per cent. There are signs of improvement. New international enrolment increased by 14 per cent this fall. But rebuilding student numbers after several years of decline will take time. In an October update , Memorial reported that total enrolment had fallen by two per cent over the past year. This happened despite increases in new undergraduate and graduate students. Memorial’s experience shows how changes in immigration policy can make long-term university planning more difficult. Why regional differences matter Atlantic Canada faces circumstances that differ greatly from Canada’s large metropolitan centres. A recent Atlantic Economic Panel report identifies an aging population and ongoing difficulties finding workers as barriers to economic growth. It also highlights the importance of immigration in sustaining population growth and addressing labour shortages. International students are not a substitute for sound immigration or workforce development policies. Not all international graduates choose to remain in Canada. Those who wish to stay must find suitable employment and meet immigration requirements. Nevertheless, post-secondary education can provide a pathway into the Canadian workforce. International students in Atlantic Canada can develop professional networks, gain local work experience and build careers in the region. A recent study in Atlantic Canada highlights the importance of immigration in sustaining population growth and addressing labour shortages. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Andrew Vaughan Falling international enrolment also affects university finances. Statistics Canada reports that international undergraduates paid an average of $41,746 in tuition in 2025–26. Canadian undergraduates paid an average of $7,734. Although fees vary by province and program, declining international enrolment can disproportionately affect university budgets. It’s been estimated that Canadian universities lost about $1 billion in annual international tuition revenue between 2023-24 and 2025-26. Further losses are projected through 2030-31. That doesn’t mean universities should depend indefinitely on international tuition to balance their budgets. Heavy reliance on one revenue source leaves institutions vulnerable when policies change . A better way to assess the policy Addressing the enrolment decline doesn’t mean returning to the previous approach to international student recruitment. Concerns about housing, student protection and the integrity of the study permit process are important. But reducing study permit numbers should not be the only measure of success. The federal government should examine why approval rates differ so sharply among provinces. It should also consider regional needs and whether universities can adequately support international students. Provincial governments and universities have responsibilities too. These include providing housing and student services, maintaining sound recruitment practices and helping graduates find employment. Read more: Canada identifies international students as ‘ideal immigrants’ but supports are lacking Canada needs policies that balance immigration goals with the unique needs of its regions. This doesn’t mean abandoning national limits; it means examining their effects and making changes where needed. Atlantic Canada’s experience shows that reducing international student numbers is not enough to judge whether a policy works. Its impacts on universities, students and the communities they serve matter too. Dale Kirby receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council.

Ottawa anticipated declines of no more than 10 per cent in several smaller provinces, including all four Atlantic provinces. It even expected an increase in Newfoundland and Labrador. Instead, approvals fell by at least 59 per cent in these provinces. The federal immigration department could not explain why approval rates fell so far below expectations. Allocating study permit applications to provinces does not guarantee that students will receive permits, accept university offers or enrol. Nor can the entire enrolment decline be blamed on the federal cap. Student applications, permit approval rates, financial pressures and Canada’s appeal as a study destination also affect enrolment. The scene at Memorial University Where I work in the faculty of education at Memorial University in Newfoundland, international enrolment fell from 4,889 students in 2023 to 2,682 in fall 2026 , a decrease of more than 45 per cent. There are signs of improvement. New international enrolment increased by 14 per cent this fall. But rebuilding student numbers after several years of decline will take time. In an October update , Memorial reported that total enrolment had fallen by two per cent over the past year. This happened despite increases in new undergraduate and graduate students. Memorial’s experience shows how changes in immigration policy can make long-term university planning more difficult. Why regional differences matter Atlantic Canada faces circumstances that differ greatly from Canada’s large metropolitan centres. A recent Atlantic Economic Panel report identifies an aging population and ongoing difficulties finding workers as barriers to economic growth. It also highlights the importance of immigration in sustaining population growth and addressing labour shortages. International students are not a substitute for sound immigration or workforce development policies. Not all international graduates choose to remain in Canada. Those who wish to stay must find suitable employment and meet immigration requirements. Nevertheless, post-secondary education can provide a pathway into the Canadian workforce. International students in Atlantic Canada can develop professional networks, gain local work experience and build careers in the region. A recent study in Atlantic Canada highlights the importance of immigration in sustaining population growth and addressing labour shortages. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Andrew Vaughan Falling international enrolment also affects university finances. Statistics Canada reports that international undergraduates paid an average of $41,746 in tuition in 2025–26. Canadian undergraduates paid an average of $7,734. Although fees vary by province and program, declining international enrolment can disproportionately affect university budgets. It’s been estimated that Canadian universities lost about $1 billion in annual international tuition revenue between 2023-24 and 2025-26. Further losses are projected through 2030-31. That doesn’t mean universities should depend indefinitely on international tuition to balance their budgets. Heavy reliance on one revenue source leaves institutions vulnerable when policies change . A better way to assess the policy Addressing the enrolment decline doesn’t mean returning to the previous approach to international student recruitment. Concerns about housing, student protection and the integrity of the study permit process are important. But reducing study permit numbers should not be the only measure of success. The federal government should examine why approval rates differ so sharply among provinces. It should also consider regional needs and whether universities can adequately support international students. Provincial governments and universities have responsibilities too. These include providing housing and student services, maintaining sound recruitment practices and helping graduates find employment. Read more: Canada identifies international students as ‘ideal immigrants’ but supports are lacking Canada needs policies that balance immigration goals with the unique needs of its regions. This doesn’t mean abandoning national limits; it means examining their effects and making changes where needed. Atlantic Canada’s experience shows that reducing international student numbers is not enough to judge whether a policy works. Its impacts on universities, students and the communities they serve matter too. Dale Kirby receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council.
articles.title: Canada’s international student cap hit Atlantic universities hard. Here’s why it matters

articles.content: Tokyo then, St. John's now? A giant squid attacks a bait squid off the coast of Tokyo in 2006. (Tsunemi Kubodera/National Science Museum of Japan) , CC BY When I learned that Netflix planned to film the miniseries Below , about a sea monster terrorizing a Newfoundland outport , I thought to myself: “THIS I’ve gotta see!” First, the series showcases coastal Newfoundland, where I was raised and live. Second, I have studied ocean life in the island’s waters for most of my career. Third, it features the marine lab where I work , the Oceans Sciences Centre. And fourth, it stars a giant squid(-ish) animal (sorry Josh Hartnett). Giant squid have a special place in Newfoundland folklore and science, from early encounters with fishermen to some of the first scientific evidence of their existence. Unveiling the giant squid One key player in this history was the Irish clergyman Moses Harvey , who moved to Newfoundland in 1852 and undertook natural history research in what was then a British colony. Harvey’s research included revealing the existence of giant squid to the world based on a specimen that washed ashore. Fishermen had brought it to him to photograph and communicate to the science community in London. Arms, tentacles and head (buccal region, including beak visible) of a giant squid from Logy Bay, Newfoundland, photographed draped over Moses Harvey’s sponge bath in November 1873. (Variously attributed to John Maunder, Moses Harvey and Messrs. McKenny and Parsons) Fast forward to the 1960s, when the founding director of the Ocean Sciences Centre, Fred Aldrich , joined the faculty at Memorial University and soon focused his career on pursuing giant squid. Although Aldrich tried to catch a living specimen, he only obtained squid that washed up on beaches. Newfoundland is one of the global hotspots where giant squid appear more frequently, every 30 years or so (New Zealand is another, attesting to giant squid affinity for cooler waters). Below ‘s arrival roughly coincides with one of those cycles. The Rooms provincial museum in St. John’s displays a preserved version of one of these amazing animals. Giant squid: Not known to be vindictive Early in the series, we meet an (oddly) barefooted marine biologist walking through the hallways of the marine lab. This scene earned a loud “ewww” from my graduate students on the grounds of hygiene as well as occupational health and safety. The biologist turns out to be the expert on giant squid and the voice of sanity when fishermen, the military and a local developer all pursue the creature (nicknamed “Mudder” by the locals, foreshadowing why she is attacking the community) with bloodlust. This marine biologist also provides impromptu medical expertise when residents fall ill from drinking ice water tainted by the animal. (Side note, DO NOT entrust your local marine biologist with urgent medical needs — we are not that type of doctor!) I could join the Facebook crowd quibbling about who got the Newfoundland accents right and who missed the mark. Or I could ask why the Coast Guard would fully abandon people living on a small, isolated island in crisis. But Below generally did a good job on the science. The biology of the animal was reasonably plausible, including its swimming skills and even its ability to survive in ice. As a (likely necessary) stretch, I thought the intellectual prowess and directed vindictiveness of the squid in the series pushed the limits of credibility, although researchers have documented some impressive abilities in cephalopods (of which giant squid are members). Still, it was a good effort to maintain scientific plausibility and fun to see marine biota as the star attraction. Historical accuracy I took a course in marine invertebrates from Aldrich when I was an undergraduate in the early 1980s. Although he was in the late stages of his career, his enthusiasm for giant squid was still evident in his lectures. He would have loved to have seen the first live footage of giant squid in the wild collected just 20 years ago by Japanese scientists, and I think he would have enjoyed watching Below and he’d be happy I’m writing about it. I certainly enjoyed watching Below , not just because of the Newfoundland setting but because it seemed entirely appropriate for the story, which was in some ways a homage to Newfoundland and its ocean history. The plot weaved in the innate capacity of local fishers to adapt and work together to solve challenges (who can “put the arse back in a cat,” as locals would say). It addressed the collapse of the northern cod fishery that threw some 37,000 Newfoundlanders out of work. And it began with a striking scene about the government’s resettlement of more than 28,000 residents of many small coastal communities to larger centres in the 1950s and '60s. It also captured the general mistrust of government in outport communities. My CFA (come from away) graduate students also appreciated seeing the “Screeching In” ceremony , and the real sense of Newfoundland conveyed by the series. Read more: The trauma caused by resettlement in Newfoundland and Labrador must be acknowledged Stoking interest in the ocean I am not a particular fan of the horror genre, though I recognize its nod to productions from decades earlier when creatures emerged from the ocean depths to wreak havoc on an unsuspecting humanity (think Godzilla , Jaws , and Orca ). Though the genre isn’t for everyone, most people I asked said they enjoyed the series, and particularly the Newfoundland ambience. I also applaud the Below team for communicating the complexity of the ocean, and their efforts to capture the imagination and interest of the public with its many unknowns. The series also underscored the ongoing potential for ocean exploration. Scientists discover thousands of new marine species every year and could discover many more if there were more of us. Many of these discoveries come from the deep sea , where giant squid spend most of their time. Most new marine species are small animals, but, as scientists sample more ocean, a surprise discovery occasionally emerges not unlike the giant squid in Below . Perhaps given Below ’s success ( the No. 1 ranked show in Canada on Netflix the week after its release , with an 87 per cent Tomatometer on Rotten Tomatoes ), Hollywood might see some potential in telling exciting stories that bring the ocean into our living rooms. That focus could inspire a new generation of scientists. I can’t help thinking that watching Jaws and Orca when I was an impressionable teen helped to push my career interests towards the ocean, where my ancestors had also earned their living. Paul Snelgrove receives funding from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Council of Canada and the Canada First Research Excellence Fund.

articles.content: Elizabeth Holmes is questioned by Nathan Fielder in 'You Can See Everything.' (A24) This story contains a spoiler about ‘You Can See Everything .’ Canadian comedian Nathan Fielder’s runaway-hit documentary You Can See Everything reintroduces audiences to Silicon Valley founder Elizabeth Holmes, who was convicted of fraud in 2022 . Holmes maintains she is innocent . Through Fielder’s lens, the film prompts us to question her conduct anew by exploring the meaning of acting, drama, truth, lies and fiction. In the film, Holmes objects to a quote of hers reported by the New York Times . According to the Times , Holmes said of actors portraying her: “They’re not playing me. They’re playing a character I created.” In Fielder’s documentary, Holmes’s husband reads the quote and says it doesn’t sound like something she would say . He suggests Holmes said instead: “They’re playing a character they created,” and she agrees. Partly through the film’s interviews with Holmes and her husband, as well as commentary by Fielder, viewers are led to wonder: Has she been playing a character she created, intended to deceive others? Is she now playing a role? Does she even know? Playing a role If Holmes is deliberately playing a role, we are inclined to condemn her as a fraudulent deceiver, well-deserving of her punishment; if not, we may be more inclined to see her sympathetically — flawed, caught up in a scheme largely wrought by others. ‘You Can See Everything’ trailer. It might seem that, because each person knows what they’re doing, they’re the authority on whether they are playing a role. But Fielder’s film, and his previous work that straddles the line between awkward comedy and social inquiry , challenges where the boundaries lie. In his HBO docuseries The Rehearsal , Fielder plays himself as a director helping people prepare for difficult situations by staging elaborate rehearsals of how they might unfold . The series leads the audience to question the relationship between the rehearsals and the real situation they mean to influence. Actions, imitations One way to think about this is by examining the difference between doing things and acting as though we’re doing them — for the ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle, the difference between an action and an imitation. To frame this issue more carefully, we can turn to a distinction Aristotle drew between “action” and “production.” For Aristotle, the arts are particular kinds of know-how. A shoemaker, for instance, knows how to produce shoes. Drama, writes Aristotle, knows how to produce the imitation ( mimēsis ) of actions . The actor’s aim is to produce a compelling imitation of someone, say, making a shoe. That imitated action is the product of the art. When done well, the audience is convinced they have seen someone do the action, perhaps briefly forgetting it was only an imitation. Often, an actor playing a shoemaker does not go so far as to make a shoe. But what if they do? ‘The Fielder Method’ The fourth episode of The Rehearsal , “The Fielder Method,” sees Fielder describe a method to train people to perform on his show. Fielder invites actors to shadow a person, called their “primary,” to learn how to imitate them in the rehearsals. He goes so far as to have them work the job of their primary or even move into a similar living arrangement. Following this method, it very well may be the case that an actor playing a shoemaker makes a real shoe. “The Fielder Method” shows that the distinction between “imitated action” and “genuine action” is porous. An audience, actor can get lost An effective imitation convinces audiences, temporarily, that we are witnessing the action, and we respond to it, at least in part, as a doing of that action. The audience can get lost in whether what they are seeing is an action or its imitation. An effective imitation, then, can be a powerful tool in the hands of someone intent on deception. Yet, as Fielder’s work also suggests, the actor can get caught up in their role. In The Rehearsal (“Pretend Daddy”), Fielder (playing himself) is rehearsing parenting a six-year old child. The child actor playing his child becomes attached to Fielder, calling him “daddy.” Fielder himself seemingly has real feelings for the child actor. If what an actor does as an imitation coincides with the actual deed so precisely that its outcome is indistinguishable from the real thing, its status hangs on what comes next: The actor’s stepping out of character and returning to “real life.” But what if the actor doesn’t step out of character? What if they leave “real life” behind? In The Rehearsal , Fielder becomes so committed to understanding pilots that he becomes one, flying a Boeing 737 from takeoff to landing. Is it plausible that Holmes, too, began intent on deception, playing a brilliant, Steve Jobs-like CEO, but then became lost in the role, increasingly unable to acknowledge distance between herself and the character she created? Or is this explanation a perfect hiding place to deny responsibility? ‘Why would I deceive you?’ A viral scene where Holmes asks Fielder, “Why would I deceive you?” is astonishing because there is such a clear reason for Holmes to deceive Fielder. In the film, partly through Fielder’s dialogue with actor Amanda Seyfried , who played Holmes in a miniseries , the film deals with how to understand Holmes. Their dialogue is interspersed with newly created scenes of Seyfried playing Holmes in Fielder’s documentary to study her, using the technique developed in The Rehearsal . One explanation could be that Holmes believes herself, or has become lost in her role. This would not excuse her crimes. But it might suggest that understanding her properly requires us to think about the role of imitation and art in our lives, just as Fielder’s works challenge us to do. On the other hand, what exactly have we seen? Commentators have raised ethical concerns around how Fielder’s relationship to his subject shapes what we do and importantly don’t see (such as the impacts of Holmes’s fraud) — or genre questions , including whether it really should be called a documentary. Read more: Can you see everything? Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes face off in You Can See Everything A compelling imitation, Aristotle tells us , is delightful because we love to learn, and imitation teaches us. This may be why scores of audiences are going to cinemas to watch an almost three-hour-long documentary . Drama can be deployed for deception, but as both Aristotle and Fielder show us, it can also be an essential vehicle for questioning our assumptions about reality. John Robert Hacker-Wright does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: How Aristotle helps us unpack the art of deception in Nathan Fielder’s ‘You Can See Everything’

articles.content: In its November budget , the federal government promises households “a boost today and a bridge to tomorrow.” But above all, the budget is a bet on business investment. Its centrepiece is the Productivity Mega Deduction , a tax incentive that allows businesses to write off the full cost of eligible capital investments. It’s expected to cost $36 billion over five years . By my calculations, only about 22 cents of every new dollar goes to affordability measures. These include not only direct household assistance but also housing, skills and immigration. As a tax policy researcher at McGill University, I read budgets for how policy choices show up in everyday economic life. Looking beyond the headline announcements reveals who benefits, how much they receive and when that assistance arrives. The highlights for households For many households, the biggest immediate effect is the continuation of existing support , including rent subsidies for low-income tenants, provincial funding for home care and mental health and food bank support. Four changes stand out. The Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit — formerly the GST credit — will provide another one-time top-up in early 2027, worth up to $339 for individuals and $679 for couples with two children, paid in full to most households earning under about $46,000. The new Build Canada Workers Benefit pays the lowest earners up to $675 more and reaches workers earning under $40,000 (about $52,000 for families), but from 2028 they will receive it only after filing their tax return. The federal caregiver credit becomes refundable from 2027, meaning it’s paid even to people who owe no tax. About 180,000 low-income caregivers who currently receive no benefit will be able to claim up to $1,260 annually. The most consequential change may not touch wallets at all. From the 2027 tax year, everyone will have a May 15 deadline to file and pay their taxes. This gives most taxpayers two additional weeks to pay, but self-employed people will have a month less to file. To illustrate how the changes could affect people in different circumstances, I have constructed five fictional household scenarios, based on the budget’s eligibility rules and benefit calculations. Scenario 1: A university student in Toronto Arjun, 20, rents in Toronto and earns $25,000 from part-time and summer jobs. Arjun will get the full grocery top-up of $339. Although he earns a low wage, he will not benefit from the higher workers benefit because full-time students are excluded. He could benefit from renewed rent subsidies only if he already receives them. He will also be able to visit national museums for free, as admission becomes permanently free for people under 25. What’s in it for him: a single payment of $339 and free museum admission. Scenario 2: A low-income family in Winnipeg Kwame and Sophie rent a house in Winnipeg and have two young children. Sophie earns $18,000 annually, while Kwame earns $2,000 from part-time work alongside caring for his mother, who has dementia. The family will receive the full $679 grocery top-up, and, by my calculations, $200 more from the new workers benefit, since Kwame’s $2,000 in earnings do not reduce the benefit. But from 2028, that benefit will come only after they file their tax return, not in payments during the year. The biggest gain is for Kwame. He has long been eligible for the caregiver credit but with too little income, he could never use it. Now that it is refundable, he receives the full $1,260 a year. Their children will also be able to visit the Canadian Museum for Human Rights for free. What’s in it for them: about $2,100 more in support the first year (with some of it paid later) and free museum admission for their children. Scenario 3: A business-owning household in Mississauga The Chows are homeowners in Mississauga, Ont., with a combined annual income of $120,000. The father, Tony, runs a catering business as a sole proprietor. They earn too much to qualify for the grocery top-up or the workers benefit. But Tony is the kind of business owner the budget’s centrepiece is built for. If he buys $40,000 of new kitchen equipment, the Productivity Mega Deduction lets him deduct the full cost in the year he buys it, rather than over several years. At a 30 per cent tax rate, that cuts his tax bill that year by about $12,000. The new May 15 deadline gives him two more weeks to pay, but a month less to file. What’s in it for them: about $12,000 less tax in the year Tony invests, more time to pay but less time to file. Scenario 4: A retired pensioner in Sudbury Lucien, 73, lives in Sudbury, Ont., and receives $45,000 annually in pension income. Lucien will receive the full $339 grocery supplement, but no new support through Old Age Security or the Guaranteed Income Supplement. Because little tax is withheld from his pension income, he owes approximately $4,000 annually. He must pay this in four quarterly instalments of about $1,000. Starting in 2028, the threshold for mandatory instalments rises to $7,500, allowing him to pay his tax bill in full when he files in May. What’s in it for him: a single payment of $339 and less paperwork. Scenario 5: A self-employed artist in Halifax Daniel, 34, is a self-employed illustrator in Halifax, earning $62,000 annually. The budget’s opening pages promise to make up to $45,000 of artistic earnings tax free. However, the measure is only a proposal to consult on a non-refundable Canada Creative Credit that, combined with the basic personal amount that everyone already gets, would cover up to $45,000 of artistic business income. If implemented, it could save Daniel up to approximately $4,000 annually in federal tax, based on my calculations. But details are not expected until spring 2027, and whether an illustrator’s work will qualify as “original and creative artistic works” is still to be decided. What’s in it for him: a potential tax benefit, but for now, a promise rather than a payment. Who benefits most? The budget’s assistance is primarily aimed at the lower-income households, particularly workers and caregivers. Much of it, however, is either a one-time payment or will not arrive until 2027 or later. Seniors, students and salaried middle-income families get little new support. Meanwhile, the biggest tax break goes to businesses that invest, and it pays off only for those that are profitable. The government is betting that greater business investment will raise incomes over time, and eventually benefit Canadians more broadly. But those gains are not guaranteed, and households facing high living costs need relief now. For now, they get a boost. The bridge to tomorrow is still under construction. It’s expected to cost $36 billion over five years . By my calculations, only about 22 cents of every new dollar goes to affordability measures. These include not only direct household assistance but also housing, skills and immigration. Looking beyond the headline announcements reveals who benefits, how much they receive and when that assistance arrives.
